documented_range.note: Built 1833 by James Kinzie — 'the first structure ever erected in the place for hotel purposes' — and standing at the north-east corner of Lake and Canal until it was moved in 1880 to 35 and 37 Milwaukee Avenue to clear the site for the Jones & Laughlin works. Both ends are attested, which is why a forty-seven-year span is tagged documented rather than being a research gap in disguise. IT IS STILL TOO LONG TO BE ONE FORM-STATE, and that is a known limitation: John Gray, landlord 1838-41, recalls 'a low one-story addition to the right, the same as on the left', so the building demonstrably grew, and nothing dates those additions. The phase should be split the moment they can be dated. A second, smaller conflict: chicagology's Green Tree page dates the move to 1880, while its Town of Chicago page, written in 1883, says the building was 'removed two years ago', i.e. 1881. Immaterial to the 1835 scene. The carpenter is disputed too — chicagology names 'Philo Cobb', DRLOIH names Silas B. Cobb, who is the historically real person and is almost certainly correct.

source_document.change_note: Prepared T-2376 incremental appearance: keep the already-adopted front ground layout and replace the old rear ell with the source-qualified open wagon bay, connector and turned boarding range. The closed-shoulder alternative remains in a separate proposal, not a version enrolled by this minimal package. Dates, geographic placement and whole-picture acceptance remain qualified.

placement.position_note:
RE-SEATED 2026-10-22 ON THE OWNER'S REPORT (T-3029): 5.80 m WEST, the northing and bearing unchanged. The owner, in the 1835 scene: "green tree tavern in 1835 is sunken, it needs to be on the ground". It was: the renderer beds a building on the lowest ground under it, and the T-0141 seat below was measured on the footprint polygon alone, while the rear ell (form.rear_ell, built since T-0083 off the east gable) runs 4.5 m further down the bank, its far corner 1.54 m from the traced waterline. Bedded to the ell's foot, the inn stood 0.58 m under its own front door; bedded to its bounding box, as the renderer then did, 0.88 m. The rule is the T-0141 rule with the whole building in it: walked west a tenth of a metre at a time, this is the first seat at which every wall foot the mesh puts on the ground, ell included, meets the modelled ground within 0.10 m, the relief 95% of the 1835 town's structures stand on. Here it is 0.099 m, and the ell's far corner stands 4.59 m from the bank. The move is inside the 20 m working uncertainty below and argues nothing new about the corner: the source still puts the inn at Lake and West Water, and the bank still decides how close to it the inn can come. The paragraphs below are the T-0141 seat as it was measured, kept as the reading this one corrects.

MOVED 2026-09-24 ON THE OWNER'S RULING OF 2026-09-21 (T-0141): from the north-east corner of Lake and Canal to the north-east corner of Lake and West Water, 116.40 m east, measured between the old east face and the new one. The northing did not change at all. THE MOVE IS ARGUED FROM THE SOURCE AND NOT FROM A PICTURE'S FRAMING. DRLOIH's article on this tavern gives the corner as 'Lake and West Water Streets'; West Water was the street that ran along the west bank while Canal lay a full plat module further west, and the owner ruled that statement preferred over the same article's gloss 'now Canal Street'. The ship masts that read beside and beyond the inn rather than above its own roofline from the `green_tree` stand (T-0122, T-0140) are the SYMPTOM that sent somebody to look at the placement; they are not a reason to move a building.

WHAT THE OLD PLACEMENT WAS, because a committed building that moves without its previous reading surviving is a town quietly rewriting itself. PLACED 2026-08-09 at EPSG:26916 E 446937.4, N 4637299.6, facade bearing 270: the west face on Canal Street's east frontage and the south face on Lake's north frontage, each half an 80 ft platted street from the modern Lake-and-Canal intersection centre read from OpenStreetMap (E 446913.0, N 4637287.4). That reading rested on chicagology's 'Northeast Corner of Lake and Canal Streets' and on DRLOIH's own body text, 'the N.E. corner of what is now Lake and Canal Streets' — both name Canal in modern terms and one says 'what is now', which is why Canal was adopted at the time. The residual was recorded then and is the thing the ruling settled: modern Canal at Lake stands about 146 m back from the modern west-bank line, so the two readings are a full plat module apart. The check that would settle it from paper is still the lot geometry on Wright 1834 or Hathaway 1834, which nobody has read.

HOW THE NEW COORDINATE IS ARRIVED AT — two constraints, one of them recomputed by tools/validate.py. (1) NORTH OF LAKE, unchanged: the south face stands 12.192 m north of the Lake-and-Canal control's northing, half the 80 ft platted module, which is the `platted_corner` derivation below and keeps the building out of Lake's platted corridor. (2) THE RIVER END: the footprint's north-east corner stands 3.01 m from the 1834 traced west bank of the South Branch (data/terrain/epochs/e1834_harbor_cut/river.geojson) — 5.71 m measured due east at that corner's own northing — and the standoff is the MODELLED GROUND'S OWN LIMIT rather than a chosen setback. The bank falls away toward the water, and a 12.19 m sill plate cannot sit level across that fall: seated hard on the bank the footprint's perimeter stands 0.88 m off the terrain beneath it, which is a building arriving nowhere and would owe a liberty. Walked west a tenth of a metre at a time, the first seat whose whole perimeter comes within the walker's 0.35 m step-up of the modelled ground is this one, at 0.294 m, with the footprint dry at all 425 samples of a 24-by-16 grid over it. So the tavern comes forward to the bank as far as the committed ground carries it, which is what 'forward to the bank' can mean here. Facade bearing is UNCHANGED at 270, due west onto West Water: F. H. Taylor's 'The fornt was on Canal street and this side was on Lake' is a claim about the street the front faced, and on the ruling's reading that street is West Water; the long elevation still runs east-west along Lake, and John Gray's second entrance is still 'on the Lake street front about the middle of the long side'. Working uncertainty about 20 m, which is the georeference's and the traced bank's and not an additional guess.

WHAT THE MOVE DISPLACED, AND ON WHOSE RULE. The committed `west_water` centreline ran through this footprint. T-0768 carried the bank offset 37.12 m past the Wolf Point turn under a stated rule — carry it until the riverward corridor reaches a committed footprint that stands ACROSS the roadway rather than beside it, and cut the line there — and the Green Tree is now the first such footprint, its nearest corner 3.01 m from the bank and its furthest 15.90 m, so it stands across the roadway exactly as James Kinzie's house does. So the line is cut at local [-20.32, -98.49]: 22.53 m shorter, ending 2.30 m south of Lake's own north platted kerb. The owner's ruling anticipated a collision and named T-0251 to settle it — the loser re-seated on its own evidence before it is withdrawn — and this line's own evidence is the rule above. The cost is written where the street is, in data/streets/1835.json: Fergus 1839's 'W. Water st north of West Lake st' again attests a street this reconstruction gives no modelled length north of Lake. Nothing already placed was displaced; the nearest committed footprint is James Kinzie's house, whose nearest corner stands 9.14 m north-west of this one.

AND THE PLATE'S COMPOSITION NOW READS, which is what T-0122 asked for and what the old placement could not give. Plate "11" of the 2026-08-11 prefire views hangs ship masts over this tavern's roofline; from the old stand the nearest water on that bearing was 157 m out and a 14.5 m mast on a 1.1 m deck needed to be inside 83 m, so the masts read beside and beyond the inn instead. The schooner moored in the reach below the forks (data/boats/era_boats.json, boat_schooner_wolf_point_2, whose own note already called this reach 'the one open water on the Green Tree Tavern's own eastward sight line') now lies 29.16 m beyond the ridge. The ridge stands 7.98 m above the building's base — 5.0 m of wall and a 38 degree gable over a 7.62 m width — which is 8.96 m on the committed heightfield, and the masthead is 15.6 m above the water. A viewer has to stand at least 0.93 of the ridge-to-mast distance back from the ridge before the masthead clears it, so the `green_tree` stand moved with the building, to Lake Street's own south platted frontage 34.85 m from the ridge on the schooner's bearing (local [-44.11, -121.52], yaw 33.3). The masthead reads 1.44 m above the roofline there, and between 1.36 m and 1.52 m for an eye anywhere from 1.6 m to 1.8 m. From the old standoff — 12.2 m off the front wall — it still does not clear, and that is geometry rather than a placement question: an 8 m ridge seen from 12 m subtends more than a 15.6 m masthead seen from 41 m, wherever the building stands.
placement.symbolic_location: North-east corner of Lake Street and West Water Street, on the west bank of the South Branch; the long elevation on Lake, the front west onto West Water, the river end on the bank as far as the modelled ground carries it.

footprint.note:
DERIVED FROM THE ATTESTED INTERIOR, not invented and not measured. This is the only footprint in the parcel with a textual basis. The arithmetic, in the original units: guest chambers 'about 12x12' feet, so a depth of two 12 ft ranks plus board partitions gives about 25 ft = 7.62 m; a hall 'divided the house' with the entrance 'about the middle of the long side', so the length is two end blocks either side of a hall of about 8 ft, and each end block must hold a 12 ft room plus partitions, giving about 40 ft = 12.19 m. The bar-room occupied one whole end, which is consistent. WHAT IS ATTESTED IS THE MODULE, NOT THE COUNT: no source gives the building's overall length or width, and a plan with three rooms rather than two on one side would make it about 52 ft. Treat the length as plus or minus about 20 per cent and the depth as firmer. The polygon is the two-storey core only — the 'low one-story addition to the right, the same as on the left' that John Gray recalls is NOT included, because its size is unattested and its date is unknown. The c. 1859 photograph (chm_green_tree_1859) would settle the overall dimensions from the proportions of a known-height building; it has not been seen.

T-2376: this polygon remains the main block's dimension/coordinate reference. The separately reconstructed left connector and gabled range are described by form.enclosed_left_annex. Their exact resolved occupied polygons are carried separately to physical consumers; the open wagon bay is not silently filled by a bounding rectangle. This does not add an archival dimension or date to the core. This model-only preparation does not yet qualify additional occupied solids or navigation/ground consumers; the main-body footprint stays unchanged until the separate compound-consumer work is verified.

stories.note: 'a two-story frame building' (DRLOIH), and chicagology's witnesses use the second floor throughout — 'a stairway in this hall led to the second floor'.

construction.note: DISPUTED, AND THE DISPUTE HAS A NAME ATTACHED TO IT. Two sources call the Green Tree a two-storey frame building outright. Against that, chicagology's Town of Chicago page reports that W. H. Stow — the man who built the Western Hotel two blocks south — 'did claim that the Green Tree was originally of logs and it was not until years afterward that it was covered with weatherboarding and given the appearance of a frame building.' Frame is adopted because it is the reading of both detailed accounts and because the interior the witnesses describe is a framed interior: board partitions, a stair hall, whitewashed plank walls, chambers laid out on a 12 ft module. The log-core claim is one man's recollection, recorded second-hand, about a rival's house, and it is carried in this record as log_core so it is not lost. Braced versus balloon is separately unattested: balloon framing appeared in Chicago in 1832-33, so an 1833 building could be either, and braced_frame is the conservative reading for the earlier date.

log_core.note: Records the rejected reading so it stays visible. W. H. Stow claimed the Green Tree was originally of logs and weatherboarded only years later. Adopted as false for the reasons in the construction note; if it is true, the 1835 building is a weatherboarded log structure rather than a frame one, which changes the wall section but not the massing, the plan or the placement.

cladding.note: Not directly attested for this building. Clapboard is the standard cladding for a frame building of this type and period, and the competing log-core account calls the covering 'weatherboarding', which is the same thing under another name — so both readings of the construction converge on a lapped horizontal board exterior.

paint.note: A CORRECTION TO A CLAIM IN CIRCULATION. The Green Tree is sometimes described as whitewashed, including in this project's own research summary, but the attested whitewash is INTERIOR: Edwin Gale writes that 'The walls, ceilings, and board partitions had evidently received a coat of whitewash when the house was built'. Nothing describes the exterior finish. Unpainted weathered clapboard is the reading adopted, and it is positively supported by the Sauganash's white paint being remarkable at Wolf Point in 1831 — if the Green Tree had been painted white two years later, the contrast the sources draw would be weaker. Not attested either way; the c. 1859 photograph would settle it.

wall_height_m.note: THE BEST-FOUNDED WALL HEIGHT IN THE DATASET, because a ceiling height is actually attested: 'Seven and one-half feet is rather low for a hotel ceiling.' Two storeys at 7 1/2 ft = 15 ft, plus floor structure between them and a sill course, gives about 16 1/2 ft = 5.0 m to the plate. The 7 1/2 ft is documented; the allowance for joists and sill is the inference.

roof_type.note: John Gray: 'There should also be a small attic window in the gable end, for we used the attic, too.' A gable end with a window in it is a direct attestation of the roof form — one of the few in this dataset that is not typological. With the front on Canal and the long side on Lake, the gable ends face east and west and the ridge runs east-west along Lake Street.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested. 38 degrees is mid-range for period gable framing and leaves an attic tall enough to lodge people in, which the sources say it did.

fenestration.note: The PANE CHARACTER is attested — a guest chamber 'about 12x12, with two windows 6x8', small-paned sash, plus 'a small attic window in the gable end'. Two windows per 12 ft chamber on a 40 x 25 ft two-storey block implies a regularly fenestrated elevation. Since T-0083 the ARRANGEMENT is carried by elevation_scheme, read off plate '11'; this value still states the pane character, which the plate agrees with — 6-over-6 sash in even bays.

elevation_scheme.note: THE BUILDING FRONTS ON A GABLE END, AND ITS EVEN BAYS RUN ALONG THE EAVES ELEVATIONS. Two halves, separately grounded. That the front is a gable end is a join of attested facts already in this record: the front on Canal (F. H. Taylor), the long side on Lake, and the gable ends facing east and west (John Gray's attic window note, and the roof_type note's own reading). The bay ARRANGEMENT — even 6-over-6 sash in regular bays along the long elevation, doors and attic lights on the gable faces — is read off plate '11' of the owner's 2026-08-11 reference set, committed at data/sources/assets/prefire_views_kevin_2026_08/p6_0.png: a tier-5 retrospective view, which may drive fenestration rhythm as inferred and may never drive a coordinate. The plate is not yet held as a source record (T-0075 owns that), so the citation is a committed path. The pictured south eaves elevation's bay count is now stated separately by eaves_bays on T-2376; the opposite elevation keeps the archetype's footprint arithmetic as a reconstruction under docs/LIBERTIES.md L152. No dimension or geographic placement is taken from the plate.

side_entrance.note: PICTURE-LED SOUTH EAVES OPENING PATTERN FOR THE 1835 MODEL, not a finding that this inn never had a side door. The held Andreas/Braunhold reproduction shows seven sash on the south long elevation on each floor, with a sash at the middle ground-floor station. The independently held original Trowbridge plate in Gale 1902, facing p.35 / scan n55, captioned 'The Green Tree Tavern in 1835', shows the same seven-bay window rhythm and no middle ground-floor door; its frontmost lower sash is partly obscured by the hanging board and people, while the middle station is visible. Setting this existing attribute to null selects the archetype's normal sash at all seven existing south-wall stations instead of substituting a door at the fourth station. The earlier John Gray testimony is retained here verbatim: 'on the Lake street front about the middle of the long side', with the hall and stairway behind it (chicagology_prefire127, transcribing the Inter Ocean, 1 July 1883; Gray kept the inn in 1838-41). That later recollection may describe a changed or schematic form, but it does not date the door to 1 July 1835, and the drawings do not prove its historical absence on that date. The choice follows the two pictured opening patterns as inferred form; exact July-1835 appearance remains uncertain. The original undated Andreas plate is not dated by the local reproduction's 1838 caption, and Trowbridge is retrospective, not an independent contemporary 1835 survey. Existing south-wall seven-bay count, even spacing, stock sash dimensions and height bands, north-wall rhythm, primary front entrance, footprint, geographic placement and all other form values stay unchanged. No c.1859 check_required photograph or Gray-derived new geometry supplies this correction; the two public-domain picture records supply the visible sash pattern.

rear_ell.note:
T-2376 retires the old rear ell as a July-1835 depiction choice. Its original position was a reconstruction made under the obsolete Canal placement, using the pictured lower wing and Gray's later testimony without a dated rear plan. The governing drawings do not resolve or show that projecting right/rear form. Gray explicitly recalls a right addition 'the same as on the left' during his 1838–41 tenancy, and the historical note promised a second wing if the Lake-and-West-Water placement won; that later bilateral testimony and the promise remain counterevidence, not proof that either addition was absent in 1835 or that both were the same pictured building. The revised model builds the pictured left connector/range, keeps the competing shoulder readings, and leaves an unverified 1835 rear/bilateral stage unmodeled rather than presenting the old placement proxy as another established wing. No historic absence, alteration date, tenant identity or room count is asserted.

HISTORICAL PRE-RETIREMENT NOTE:
THE LOW ADDITION, BUILT AT THE REAR AND DECLARED. John Gray, landlord 1838-41, attests 'a low one-story addition to the right, the same as on the left'; the 1838 Braunhold engraving (owner_brief_2026_08_18 README, image 6) draws 'a lower gabled wing at the left with a wide (carriage) door', and plate '11' (prefire_views_kevin_2026_08/p6_0.png) draws the low gabled wing with the ship masts behind it. WHETHER A WING STOOD ON 1835-07-01 IS NOT ATTESTED — Gray describes the house three to six years after the scene date — so this is a reconstruction under the owner's 2026-08-18 standing ruling, sized by the views and claimed at docs/LIBERTIES.md L152. WHY THE REAR END AND ONLY THE REAR: Gray names additions at BOTH ends, but this record's committed placement puts the west face ON Canal Street's east frontage with zero offset, so the street end has no ground to build on — only the east (rear, yard) end does. That asymmetry is itself evidence worth recording: a west wing fits the ground only under the 'Lake and West Water' placement reading the position note carries as this record's largest residual uncertainty. If that reading ever wins, the second wing goes up with the move. The wing the views draw beside masts is consistent with either.

gallery.note: NO EVIDENCE EITHER WAY, and unlike the Sauganash there is no retrospective depiction in the project's hands to reason from. The witnesses describe two entrances — the front on Canal and one 'about the middle of the long side' on Lake — without mentioning a porch, veranda or gallery, which is weak negative evidence at best, since they were correcting a drawing rather than inventorying the elevation. False is the default, not a finding. The c. 1859 photograph (chm_green_tree_1859) settles this the moment anyone opens it.

side_additions.note: John Gray, landlord 1838-41, correcting a drawing of the house: 'There should also be a low one-story addition to the right, the same as on the left.' So by the end of the 1830s the two-storey core had a low single-storey addition at each end. WHETHER THEY EXISTED ON 1835-07-01 IS NOT ATTESTED — Gray's testimony describes the building three to six years after the scene date — which is why this is inferred and why the additions stay out of the footprint polygon. SINCE T-0083 the rear (east) one is BUILT, at the reconstructed tier, as form.rear_ell — see that attribute for why only the rear end has ground to build on. This value stays the testimony record for BOTH ends; the street-end addition remains unbuilt.

chimneys.note: Not attested in text. A tavern with a bar-room at one end, a parlour, a dining room clearable for dancing and chambers above needed more than one fireplace, and two stacks is the normal disposition for a 40 ft block with a central hall. The number is inference — and since T-0083 it agrees with plate '11', which draws exactly two. WHERE they stand is carried by chimney_placement.

persons.name: Chester Ingersoll
persons.note: A DOCUMENTED RESIDENT IN A CONTEMPORARY NEWSPAPER, which is worth more than any amount of Andreas. Two further things fix him in the town in this period: his house was the district polling place on 9 December 1833, and a travelling ventriloquist named Kenworthy advertised in the Democrat of 10 June 1834 the close of an engagement at 'the Travelers' Home, a hotel kept by Chester Ingersoll, on Wolf Point'. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 2 times, as “INGERSOLL CHESTER”, 1833-10-24 to 1835-06-26: 1 federal land entry — SW sec 28 T39N R13E and 1 parcel of the school section — BL37 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read, 163.79 acres stated in all, for $253.10 (ls0246, ls0849). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: INGERSOLL CHESTER matches Chester Ingersoll: the forename names Chester Ingersoll of the 1 person of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

Its four inside corners were computed for this parcel from modern OpenStreetMap intersection centres fetched 2026-08-11, offset 12.2 m into the block on each axis, half of an 80 ft street per Hathaway 1834: NW 447538.25 / 4637130.78, NE 447639.27 / 4637130.25, SW 447541.20 / 4637018.49, SE 447639.80 / 4637018.05, which makes the block about 101 x 112 m. The jail's own north-west corner is set on the square's north-west corner, so the footprint origin - which is the building's south-west corner - sits its own depth south of it. footprint.note: INVENTED. NO SOURCE REACHED GIVES THIS BUILDING A DIMENSION, a plan, or a number of cells. 6.096 x 4.572 m is 20 x 15 ft, recorded converted with the original figures stated per data/datum.json's units rule. The only constraint the evidence offers is relative and it runs in both directions: the jail was built because something more metropolitan was required than the estray pen, so it is a more substantial thing than a stock pound; and it was itself superseded within a few years, so it was small. Nothing else about the shape is a finding: the plain rectangle, the proportion and the scale are all this record's.

construction.note: The building is named a LOG jail in the only description this project has of it, which makes the material the single best-attested thing about it. THE PLATE NOW SETTLES THE SECOND HALF OF IT: the engraving of the first Cook County jail in the owner's 2026-08-18 brief (data/sources/assets/owner_brief_2026_08_18/README.md, image 1) draws squared timber laid horizontally — 'a low log jail — squared timber, near-flat roof' — which is hewn log in courses with notched corners, exactly what this archetype builds for this value (generators/common/logwork.py). Until 2026-08-21 this note said hewn-versus-round was unattested and the archetype's hewn wall was a convention standing where evidence should be; the plate is that evidence, at tier 5, for the FABRIC and not for any dimension. Whether the walls were single or doubled, and whether they were lined inside, nothing reached says. The plate is a TIER 5 PICTORIAL held here as the brief's written record rather than a committed binary — the images were supplied in-session and T-0075 owns identifying them against the Andreas plate numbering and creating the source record — so it is cited by path, the way this dataset's other brief-driven attributes are (green_tree_tavern chimneys, image 6). The value's own grade is unchanged: 'log' was attested by Andreas before the plate and still is.

roof_type.note: The detailed public-domain Gale/Trowbridge 1902 plate, captioned 1836, depicts a gabled log core behind the palisade. This replaces the earlier roof choice based on a written near-flat summary. Andreas 1884 depicts a conflicting hip/pyramidal cap; that independent picture is retained as a source disagreement. Applying the depicted form to July 1835 is a declared continuity reconstruction, not a claim that the plate depicts July.

roof_pitch_deg.note: One bounded 28-degree reconstruction of the visibly pitched gable in the full Gale 1902 plate. On the unchanged reconstructed 4.572 m span it rises 1.216 m, rather than the previous 0.486 m cap. The drawing supplies the taller roof form, not a measured angle, a metric plan or proof of its July 1835 state. The differing Andreas cap does not become a second building.

wall_height_m.note: A finite 3.35 m eave choice exposes 0.91 m of core above the existing reconstructed 2.44 m palisade, as both retrospective pictures show a substantial log block above the enclosure. This replaces the previous archetype-default 2.66 m choice, which hid almost all wall fabric. Neither plate measures metres; exact height and July continuity are reconstruction. No footprint, site coordinate, street control, storey count or separate later cell is added.

door.note: Not attested. `door` in this archetype names what has to get through the opening rather than whether there was one. A jail takes a person through in hand and nothing else - no horse, no wagon - so the man-door class is the reading, and it is the only one whose 1.88 m clear height fits under this wall. Where the door stood, what it was made of, and whether it was barred or grated is not attested and is the archetype's default.

picture_layout.note: The detailed public-domain 1902 plate shows one upright barred-looking light in the log gable beside the keeper house. The light sits on the east end facing the keeper-house side: 0.48 x 0.85 m dark recess, three uprights, one horizontal crossbar, 55 mm frame, head 0.73 m above eave. These metric choices, count of uprights, material, compass and July continuity are not measured or attested. The opening does not assert a second storey or hay loft. Other outbuildings retain their default layout.

function.note: Purpose-built for confinement, and it is the building that ended the practice recorded on the estray_pen record - prisoners held in the stock pound for want of anywhere else. Cook County was organised in 1831 and the county's business was conducted in rented rooms; this is the first purpose-built county structure of any kind and it precedes the court-house on the same block by about two years.

document.research_note:
CURRENT T-2380 COMPLETION CHOICE, 2026-11-10. Adopt the detailed, independently public-domain Gale/Trowbridge 1902 depiction for the existing log core: retain its gable, expose substantial hewn wall above the 2.44 m palisade with a reconstructed 3.35 m eave and 28-degree pitch, and represent its one upright barred-looking gable light. These are bounded appearance/continuity choices for the July scene, not historical measurements or proof that every 1836-captioned feature stood by July 1835. Andreas’s hip/pyramidal cap and different keeper elevation remain a contradictory retrospective depiction, within tolerance under T-3153 rather than a demand for two inconsistent simultaneous roofs. Do not backdate the fall 1835 courthouse or invent a separate later oaken cell. All geographic/survey/phase-date/footprint facts are retained. The existing enclosure and keeper geometry are unchanged. Actual refreshed full Gale and Andreas comparisons of the adopted native core were directly reviewed on2026-11-10 and accepted underT3153 with explicit source/date/camera limits. The visible upright inset is confirmed; thin bar/crossbar legibility at the oblique diagnostic is within tolerance, not claimed sharp. Published terrain/street/Record checks are a separate parent runtime review. The UCR copy-specific rights hold is unchanged; geometry uses the independently verified public-domain 1902 artwork.

DATED HISTORY BELOW: older no-change, low-roof and open-ticket statements describe preceding increments and are superseded by the current paragraph and current form attributes.

CURRENT COMPOUND INCREMENT: John Beach's separate keeper house, a continuous pointed palisade front and a low braced hung gate are represented as one source-informed continuity reconstruction. Gale1902 p51 places the house partly within the enclosure facing Randolph during an1835-framed recollection; the accompanying plate explicitly says1836. Neither source supplies a metric site plan or proves this exact July1835 state. The domestic house supersedes the older one-roof/open-square assertion. The original log-cell geometry and shallow12degree roof remain unchanged, with a1.30m southward reconstructed access setback explicitly declared in position.note. The Gale comparison still differs in exposed rear-core roof and compound proportions; Andreas shows a conflicting shallow cap and different house elevation. T-2380 stays open and no picture match or geographic camera is claimed. The verified1902 US publication supplies public-domain artwork; the separately catalogued UCR copy retains its own credit and copy-specific hold.

 DATED HISTORICAL SOURCE AND MODEL RATIONALES FOLLOW, preserved from the preceding record; older statements of no new placement or a sole roof are superseded by the current paragraph and phase change_note.

 CURRENT IMAGE EVIDENCE: The exact detailed jail drawing is verified in Edwin O. Gale’s 1902 book, illustrated by W. E. S. Trowbridge. Its actual title and copyright pages establish a public-domain publication; the earlier artwork-level hold below is superseded. The separate UCR copy is catalogued Date Created and/or Issued 19 September 1930, which still does not establish publication in 1930 or an item-specific reuse licence. Its required credit is Keystone-Mast Collection, UCR/California Museum of Photography, University of California at Riverside. Use the independently verified 1902 plate as the artwork source. The caption describes 1836, and the jail core is mostly concealed by its palisade; exact July 1835 form and component continuity remain unresolved. This correction derives no new geometry or asset from the UCR copy and changes no building form.

HISTORICAL MODEL RATIONALE AND DATED SOURCE REASSESSMENTS FOLLOW.

A DOCUMENTED BUILDING WITH ONE DOCUMENTED ATTRIBUTE. What is attested is that it was a jail, that it was of logs, that it went up in the fall of 1833, and that it stood at the north-west corner of the court-house square. Everything else in this record - every dimension, the roof, the wall height, the door, the bearing - is inference or invention, and the confidence view will show it as such. THE RECORD IS WORTH HAVING ANYWAY, and this is the clearest case in the parcel for the working policy behind it: on 1835-07-01 the public square carried the jail and the roofless estray pen; the brick courthouse was not erected until the fall of 1835. The earlier three-building conjecture is superseded by this record’s phase change_note and the actual Andreas page176. ARCHETYPE CHOICE: outbuilding rather than log_dwelling, and the difference is not cosmetic. log_dwelling reads a storey count, a loft, a chimney count and a sign, and builds a dwelling's openings; outbuilding builds a plain box with one door sized by what has to get through it, and refuses a storey count outright. A jail is the second of those. The archetype's own family list - stable, shed, barn, smokehouse, privy, crib, woodshed - does not name a jail, and that is a gap in the vocabulary rather than a reason to build the wrong thing. WHAT THE PLATE ADDED, 2026-08-21 (T-0070, the owner asking that the jail 'should be made more accurate' to its engraving): a tier-5 pictorial of this building, written up as image 1 of the 2026-08-18 brief, which the record did not have when it was placed. It reached two attributes and no others. The roof came down from the archetype's 32-degree gable default to 12 degrees, because the plate draws a near-flat roof and a convention loses to a picture of the thing itself; the construction note stopped calling hewn-versus-round unattested, because the plate draws squared timber laid horizontally. It reached NEITHER dimension nor coordinate, and it may not: a tier-5 pictorial drives form, materials and massing as inferred and never a footprint outline or a position. So the footprint is still invented and still says so. WHAT WOULD UPGRADE THIS RECORD, in order of value: any county order or contract for the jail's construction, which is the kind of document that carries a dimension, a cost or a specification for the logs; Andreas vol. 1 at page-image level around scan pp. 367 and 1243, which is where the prose transcribed into this project's dossier sits; and the Cook County Sheriff's own published jail history, cited in the dossier and not yet held as a source record here.

1902 PUBLICATION FOUND — T-2380, LATER SAME-DAY SUPERSESSION (2026-10-23). The exact detailed jail artwork has now been actually read in Edwin O. Gale’s 1902Reminiscences of Early Chicago and Vicinity, plate facing printed p53, source trowbridge_first_jail_gale_1902. Actual title credits ILLUSTRATED BY W.E.S.TROWBRIDGE and Fleming H. Revell Company, Chicago/New York/Toronto, MCMII; actual copyright page states 1902 and October. The independently published 1902artwork is public domain by age and unblocks project picture work from that plate. It supersedes the earlier artwork-level hold, without assuming publication from UCR’s 1930 combined date or clearing later copy-specific additions. The UCR catalogue remains check_required/text_only with its required credit retained. No school/Tremont permission is being extended to the jail.

NARRATIVE AND SCENE DATE REMAIN BOUNDED. Gale p25 dates arrival to 25 May 1835; p43 starts the early-morning town stroll; p51 says a small log jail is concealed by a high plank palisade and John Beach occupies a house partly in that enclosure facing Randolph. The courthouse is “just started.” Pages 52–55 continue the stroll and give no jail alteration sequence. This is a 1902 recollection framed in 1835, while the actual plate explicitly says 1836. It supports the jail/keeper-house distinction but does not measure the core or prove every pictured detail existed by 1 July 1835. The independent Andreas hip-roof contrast and separate-oaken-cell question remain. No form, dimensions, source linkage from a form attribute, date, confidence, placement or recipe changes here; earlier numeric geometry proposals remain unapplied pending actual model review. T-2380 stays open.

INDEPENDENT PUBLIC-DOMAIN CONTRAST. The actual Andreas’s 1884 History of Chicago vol.1 pages 175–177 were read. Page 175 distinguishes the first 1833 log jail from a later, separate oaken cell without dating the addition. Page 176 dates the first brick courthouse to FALL 1835, after the target 1 July scene. The plate on page 177, Copyright secured by A.T.Andreas 1884, shows a low house/stockade and a rear log block under a shallow hip/pyramidal cap; the same artwork is explicitly captioned FIRST COURT HOUSE AND JAIL in Andreas’s 1884 History of Cook County page 353. This confirms the jail ensemble, but not which pictured cell is the original 1833 core, its July 1835 appearance or an absolute eave/pitch. It conflicts with the taller gable in the rights-held detailed drawing. The existing model remains a provisional proxy; no roof, height, opening, date, placement or confidence value is altered by this metadata correction. T-2380 remains open.

Until 2026-08-21 this note said hewn-versus-round was unattested and the archetype's hewn wall was a convention standing where evidence should be; the plate is that evidence, at tier 5, for the FABRIC and not for any dimension. Whether the walls were single or doubled, and whether they were lined inside, nothing reached says. The plate is a TIER 5 PICTORIAL held here as the brief's written record rather than a committed binary — the images were supplied in-session and T-0075 owns identifying them against the Andreas plate numbering and creating the source record — so it is cited by path, the way this dataset's other brief-driven attributes are (green_tree_tavern chimneys, image 6). The value's own grade is unchanged: 'log' was attested by Andreas before the plate and still is.

roof_type.note: The detailed public-domain Gale/Trowbridge 1902 plate, captioned 1836, depicts a gabled log core behind the palisade. This replaces the earlier roof choice based on a written near-flat summary. Andreas 1884 depicts a conflicting hip/pyramidal cap; that independent picture is retained as a source disagreement. Applying the depicted form to July 1835 is a declared continuity reconstruction, not a claim that the plate depicts July.

roof_pitch_deg.note: One bounded 28-degree reconstruction of the visibly pitched gable in the full Gale 1902 plate. On the unchanged reconstructed 4.572 m span it rises 1.216 m, rather than the previous 0.486 m cap. The drawing supplies the taller roof form, not a measured angle, a metric plan or proof of its July 1835 state. The differing Andreas cap does not become a second building.

wall_height_m.note: A finite 3.35 m eave choice exposes 0.91 m of core above the existing reconstructed 2.44 m palisade, as both retrospective pictures show a substantial log block above the enclosure. This replaces the previous archetype-default 2.66 m choice, which hid almost all wall fabric. Neither plate measures metres; exact height and July continuity are reconstruction. No footprint, site coordinate, street control, storey count or separate later cell is added.

door.note: Not attested. `door` in this archetype names what has to get through the opening rather than whether there was one. A jail takes a person through in hand and nothing else - no horse, no wagon - so the man-door class is the reading, and it is the only one whose 1.88 m clear height fits under this wall. Where the door stood, what it was made of, and whether it was barred or grated is not attested and is the archetype's default.

picture_layout.note: The detailed public-domain 1902 plate shows one upright barred-looking light in the log gable beside the keeper house. The light sits on the east end facing the keeper-house side: 0.48 x 0.85 m dark recess, three uprights, one horizontal crossbar, 55 mm frame, head 0.73 m above eave. These metric choices, count of uprights, material, compass and July continuity are not measured or attested. The opening does not assert a second storey or hay loft. Other outbuildings retain their default layout.

function.note: Purpose-built for confinement, and it is the building that ended the practice recorded on the estray_pen record - prisoners held in the stock pound for want of anywhere else. Cook County was organised in 1831 and the county's business was conducted in rented rooms; this is the first purpose-built county structure of any kind and it precedes the court-house on the same block by about two years.

built.note: Andreas: the log jail was built in the fall of 1833.

source_document.research_note:
CURRENT T-2380 COMPLETION CHOICE, 2026-11-10. Adopt the detailed, independently public-domain Gale/Trowbridge 1902 depiction for the existing log core: retain its gable, expose substantial hewn wall above the 2.44 m palisade with a reconstructed 3.35 m eave and 28-degree pitch, and represent its one upright barred-looking gable light. These are bounded appearance/continuity choices for the July scene, not historical measurements or proof that every 1836-captioned feature stood by July 1835. Andreas’s hip/pyramidal cap and different keeper elevation remain a contradictory retrospective depiction, within tolerance under T-3153 rather than a demand for two inconsistent simultaneous roofs. Do not backdate the fall 1835 courthouse or invent a separate later oaken cell. All geographic/survey/phase-date/footprint facts are retained. The existing enclosure and keeper geometry are unchanged. Actual refreshed full Gale and Andreas comparisons of the adopted native core were directly reviewed on2026-11-10 and accepted underT3153 with explicit source/date/camera limits. The visible upright inset is confirmed; thin bar/crossbar legibility at the oblique diagnostic is within tolerance, not claimed sharp. Published terrain/street/Record checks are a separate parent runtime review. The UCR copy-specific rights hold is unchanged; geometry uses the independently verified public-domain 1902 artwork.

DATED HISTORY BELOW: older no-change, low-roof and open-ticket statements describe preceding increments and are superseded by the current paragraph and current form attributes.

CURRENT COMPOUND INCREMENT: John Beach's separate keeper house, a continuous pointed palisade front and a low braced hung gate are represented as one source-informed continuity reconstruction. Gale1902 p51 places the house partly within the enclosure facing Randolph during an1835-framed recollection; the accompanying plate explicitly says1836. Neither source supplies a metric site plan or proves this exact July1835 state. The domestic house supersedes the older one-roof/open-square assertion. The original log-cell geometry and shallow12degree roof remain unchanged, with a1.30m southward reconstructed access setback explicitly declared in position.note. The Gale comparison still differs in exposed rear-core roof and compound proportions; Andreas shows a conflicting shallow cap and different house elevation. T-2380 stays open and no picture match or geographic camera is claimed. The verified1902 US publication supplies public-domain artwork; the separately catalogued UCR copy retains its own credit and copy-specific hold.

 DATED HISTORICAL SOURCE AND MODEL RATIONALES FOLLOW, preserved from the preceding record; older statements of no new placement or a sole roof are superseded by the current paragraph and phase change_note.

 CURRENT IMAGE EVIDENCE: The exact detailed jail drawing is verified in Edwin O. Gale’s 1902 book, illustrated by W. E. S. Trowbridge. Its actual title and copyright pages establish a public-domain publication; the earlier artwork-level hold below is superseded. The separate UCR copy is catalogued Date Created and/or Issued 19 September 1930, which still does not establish publication in 1930 or an item-specific reuse licence. Its required credit is Keystone-Mast Collection, UCR/California Museum of Photography, University of California at Riverside. Use the independently verified 1902 plate as the artwork source. The caption describes 1836, and the jail core is mostly concealed by its palisade; exact July 1835 form and component continuity remain unresolved. This correction derives no new geometry or asset from the UCR copy and changes no building form.

HISTORICAL MODEL RATIONALE AND DATED SOURCE REASSESSMENTS FOLLOW.

A DOCUMENTED BUILDING WITH ONE DOCUMENTED ATTRIBUTE. What is attested is that it was a jail, that it was of logs, that it went up in the fall of 1833, and that it stood at the north-west corner of the court-house square. Everything else in this record - every dimension, the roof, the wall height, the door, the bearing - is inference or invention, and the confidence view will show it as such. THE RECORD IS WORTH HAVING ANYWAY, and this is the clearest case in the parcel for the working policy behind it: on 1835-07-01 the public square carried the jail and the roofless estray pen; the brick courthouse was not erected until the fall of 1835. The earlier three-building conjecture is superseded by this record’s phase change_note and the actual Andreas page176. ARCHETYPE CHOICE: outbuilding rather than log_dwelling, and the difference is not cosmetic. log_dwelling reads a storey count, a loft, a chimney count and a sign, and builds a dwelling's openings; outbuilding builds a plain box with one door sized by what has to get through it, and refuses a storey count outright. A jail is the second of those. The archetype's own family list - stable, shed, barn, smokehouse, privy, crib, woodshed - does not name a jail, and that is a gap in the vocabulary rather than a reason to build the wrong thing. WHAT THE PLATE ADDED, 2026-08-21 (T-0070, the owner asking that the jail 'should be made more accurate' to its engraving): a tier-5 pictorial of this building, written up as image 1 of the 2026-08-18 brief, which the record did not have when it was placed. It reached two attributes and no others. The roof came down from the archetype's 32-degree gable default to 12 degrees, because the plate draws a near-flat roof and a convention loses to a picture of the thing itself; the construction note stopped calling hewn-versus-round unattested, because the plate draws squared timber laid horizontally. It reached NEITHER dimension nor coordinate, and it may not: a tier-5 pictorial drives form, materials and massing as inferred and never a footprint outline or a position. So the footprint is still invented and still says so. WHAT WOULD UPGRADE THIS RECORD, in order of value: any county order or contract for the jail's construction, which is the kind of document that carries a dimension, a cost or a specification for the logs; Andreas vol. 1 at page-image level around scan pp. 367 and 1243, which is where the prose transcribed into this project's dossier sits; and the Cook County Sheriff's own published jail history, cited in the dossier and not yet held as a source record here.

1902 PUBLICATION FOUND — T-2380, LATER SAME-DAY SUPERSESSION (2026-10-23). The exact detailed jail artwork has now been actually read in Edwin O. Gale’s 1902Reminiscences of Early Chicago and Vicinity, plate facing printed p53, source trowbridge_first_jail_gale_1902. Actual title credits ILLUSTRATED BY W.E.S.TROWBRIDGE and Fleming H. Revell Company, Chicago/New York/Toronto, MCMII; actual copyright page states 1902 and October. The independently published 1902artwork is public domain by age and unblocks project picture work from that plate. It supersedes the earlier artwork-level hold, without assuming publication from UCR’s 1930 combined date or clearing later copy-specific additions. The UCR catalogue remains check_required/text_only with its required credit retained. No school/Tremont permission is being extended to the jail.

NARRATIVE AND SCENE DATE REMAIN BOUNDED. Gale p25 dates arrival to 25 May 1835; p43 starts the early-morning town stroll; p51 says a small log jail is concealed by a high plank palisade and John Beach occupies a house partly in that enclosure facing Randolph. The courthouse is “just started.” Pages 52–55 continue the stroll and give no jail alteration sequence. This is a 1902 recollection framed in 1835, while the actual plate explicitly says 1836. It supports the jail/keeper-house distinction but does not measure the core or prove every pictured detail existed by 1 July 1835. The independent Andreas hip-roof contrast and separate-oaken-cell question remain. No form, dimensions, source linkage from a form attribute, date, confidence, placement or recipe changes here; earlier numeric geometry proposals remain unapplied pending actual model review. T-2380 stays open.

INDEPENDENT PUBLIC-DOMAIN CONTRAST. The actual Andreas’s 1884 History of Chicago vol.1 pages 175–177 were read. Page 175 distinguishes the first 1833 log jail from a later, separate oaken cell without dating the addition. Page 176 dates the first brick courthouse to FALL 1835, after the target 1 July scene. The plate on page 177, Copyright secured by A.T.Andreas 1884, shows a low house/stockade and a rear log block under a shallow hip/pyramidal cap; the same artwork is explicitly captioned FIRST COURT HOUSE AND JAIL in Andreas’s 1884 History of Cook County page 353. This confirms the jail ensemble, but not which pictured cell is the original 1833 core, its July 1835 appearance or an absolute eave/pitch. It conflicts with the taller gable in the rights-held detailed drawing. The existing model remains a provisional proxy; no roof, height, opening, date, placement or confidence value is altered by this metadata correction. T-2380 remains open.

document.name: Sauganash Hotel

grade.why: Pictured: 3 of the pictures on the Images tab show it.

documented_range.note: Wau-Bun, describing 1831: 'a house just completed by Mark Beaubien.' Destroyed by fire 4 March 1851. The 1838 rename to Chicago Hotel and the 1837 arrival of the Chicago Theatre Company in the dining room are changes of use, not of form, so they do not open a new phase.

document.change_note: Two-story frame block built onto the log core at the Lake and Market corner, 1831; the whole then known as the Sauganash Hotel, Chicago's first hotel.

placement.position_note: PLACED 2026-08-09. The corner is documented — chicagology and the Chicago Landmark record both put the Sauganash at the south-east corner of Lake and Market — but the COORDINATE is inferred, so the tag follows the weaker half. Method: Market Street is today's N Wacker Drive and Lake Street is unchanged, an equivalence the research dossier states and the georeference independently corroborates, since the 1834 plats warped onto the modern street centrelines at 17.5 m RMS. The modern intersection centre was read from OpenStreetMap (EPSG:26916 E 447161.9, N 4637285.4) and the footprint origin offset 12.2 m east and 20.2 m south of it: half of an 80 ft platted street to reach the kerb, and the footprint's own 8 m depth so the building's north face sits on the Lake Street frontage of a south-east corner lot. Working uncertainty about 20 m, which is the georeference's, not an additional guess. Facade bearing 0 (north, onto Lake Street): the sources say it faced the forks to the north-west, so the true bearing is likely nearer 315, but the plat lot lines are orthogonal and a corner building fronting Lake is the defensible reading until better evidence appears.
placement.symbolic_location: South-east corner of Lake Street and Market Street (today Lake St and N Wacker Dr).

footprint.note: THE TWO-MASS PLAN, AND THE 12 x 8 m PLACEHOLDER IS RETIRED (T-0626, spending T-0617's reading). THE FRONTAGE IS DERIVED AND THE DEPTH IS NOT, and the block is graded at the weaker of the two. FRONTAGE 9.92 m: Braunhold's engraving draws five bays on the street face and rectified against that face's own vanishing point the five are EQUAL to 2.4 % (tools/measure_sauganash_plate.py, bay_rhythm.rectified_gaps 0.997 / 1.011 / 1.020 / 0.972). The bay measures 1.984 m at the plate's stated scale datum — a standing adult at 1.70 m, hat included, the two men on the walk reading 147 and 143 px — so five bays are 9.92 m. THE DATUM'S BIAS IS SMALL AND BOUNDED, which is what makes this a measurement rather than a floor: the men stand a pace forward of the wall, and the plate's own focal length puts them 43.0 m from the station (f 3664.7 px on a 145 px figure of 1.70 m), so a pace is 2.7 %. The frontage is therefore 9.9-10.2 m and 12 m IS REFUTED rather than merely unsupported. The value taken is the measured 9.92 and is not fudged up into the correction. What does still move it is the 1.70 m datum itself: at 1.60 m the frontage reads 9.3 m and at 1.80 m 10.5 m. DEPTH 8.0 m IS UNCHANGED AND IS STILL A RECONSTRUCTION. One plate gives no depth (docs/RESEARCH/sauganash_image_accuracy.md row 11), so nothing has measured it; it is held at the placeholder's own figure deliberately, because the placement above offsets this origin by the footprint's own 8 m depth to stand the north face on the Lake Street frontage, and moving a number with no evidence behind it would move the building. THE SECOND MASS IS NOT IN THIS POLYGON, on the precedent green_tree_tavern's rear ell set: an attached wing is the archetype's, sized by this phase's own form attributes (cross_wing, cross_wing_depth_m, cross_wing_end), and the polygon is the main block's plan. NOTE ON WHAT THIS TAG MEANS: conjectural here is about SIZE, not about existence or character. That the building was a two-storey white frame block is documented (Wau-Bun); how big it was is measured off one retrospective sheet and no better. The renderer therefore does NOT dither the massing on account of this tag — see generators/archetypes/frame_tavern.py — and the dimensional uncertainty is carried in the sidecar instead.

construction.note: Balloon framing was developed in Chicago in 1832-33 and became the dominant local method. This building predates that by a year, so balloon framing is the LESS likely reading: a braced frame built onto a log core is more probable for 1831. Flagged for correction — the value is retained only until the framing question is researched, and it should probably become braced_frame. Do not treat this as settled.

cross_wing.note: THE SECOND TWO-STOREY MASS, AND THE PLATE PROVES IT BY ARITHMETIC. The owner reported it missing on 2026-09-03 from the dev preview: 'i think there is a structure missing but you have it on the front and they have it on the rear in pictures, and it looks like the full height of the main building and similar design as the main building appears to be almost the same size, it connects from the back and side in the images.' T-0617 measured the near apex at (648, 350) with one line running out of it at image slope -0.318 and one at +0.095, and called the right-hand one a ridge on the strength of the asymmetry alone. T-0626 finished the sum. Project each line onto the vertical through the vanishing point of the plane it lies in — the plate gives both horizontal vanishing points and its own focal length, recovered from their orthogonality — and BOTH come out horizontal in the world: 1.35 deg and 0.11 deg, where a 38 deg rake in the same plane would have been DRAWN at image slope -1.99 against the -0.318 measured. So they are two RIDGES meeting at one apex, not a ridge and a rake, and the mass the owner reported is on the sheet as a measurement rather than as an impression. tools/sauganash_apex_lines.py is that arithmetic and tools/check.sh gates on it. THE SHARED APEX IS ALSO WHAT SIZES THE WING: two gable ridges of one wall height and one pitch meet at a point only when they span the same width, so the wing's span is this block's own depth and the archetype refuses to build it at any other. GRADE. One sheet — Braunhold's. The Petford watercolour and the Trowbridge drawing are the same composition from the same station, so they copy it rather than corroborate it (docs/RESEARCH/sauganash_image_accuracy.md section 1), and a tier-5 retrospective that passes its own perspective test may be read for PROPORTION and never for a coordinate. CITED ON BRAUNHOLD ALONE. The Petford and Trowbridge views were dropped from this row on 2026-09-04 for the reason the reading itself gives: they are the same composition from the same station, so listing them would dress a copy as a corroboration. The earlier separate rights concern is now superseded by verified 1902 publication, but the dependence argument still applies: a later copy is not independent corroboration.

The lot decides. This phase's placement stands the block's WEST face on Market Street's east kerb line at a 0 m setback, so a wing at the west end would stand in Market Street. It goes at the EAST end — x_max in the archetype's local frame — which is also the end the log annex already stands against: data/structures/philo_carpenter_log_shop.json is set hard on this block's east face, by the same elimination and stated there since 2026-08-11. NO SOURCES ON THIS ROW, DELIBERATELY: it cites nothing because it rests on nothing new. The plat equivalence, the kerb line and the 0 m setback are all this phase's own position block, which carries its sources; repeating them here would claim a second, independent standing this row does not have.

function.note:
A tavern from 1829 and a hotel from 1831; the social centre of the settlement in the target window. Chicago's first billiard table in a public house stood here.

THE HOUSE IS OPEN, AND FRESHLY DONE UP, THREE WEEKS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE. Reviewing the town's public houses against Detroit's new American Hotel, the Chicago Democrat of 10 June 1835, page 2 column 5, claim chicago_democrat_1835_06_10#c001, reports that 'The Sauganash has been re[paired,] fitted up and furnished with neatness and [taste,] and so far as it goes, will[, we have no doubt,] be found just the thing'. That is the only dated statement of this building's CONDITION the corpus holds, and it bears on how the scene should read it: on 1835-07-01 the Sauganash is a working, recently refitted public house and not the shabby survivor its 1829 log origins invite. 'so far as it goes' is the editor's qualification and it means small — his complaint in the same paragraph is that no establishment in Chicago is 'sufficiently extensive'. The refit is recorded here rather than in the form block below because nothing in it names a fabric, a storey or a colour, and inventing one from 'fitted up' is exactly the supply this project refuses.

occupants.note: The Beaubiens owned it until 1834; the hotel chronology gives 'Davis (1835)' as operator, possibly the John Davis running the Steamboat Hotel on North Water Street. Mark Beaubien himself had moved on by the scene date — he built the Exchange Coffee House at Lake and Wells in 1834. The 1835 proprietor is a lead, not a settled fact.

PRIOR RESEARCH RECORD:
MILESTONE 0 REFERENCE RECORD. Two things are documented and vivid — the white two-story frame and the bright-blue shutters, both from Wau-Bun — and two things are unknown: the building's dimensions and whether it had a gallery. That combination is exactly why the per-attribute confidence model exists, and this record is deliberately the first one in the dataset. See docs/RESEARCH/sauganash_hotel.md for the source conflicts and the reasoning behind each reading. The Wigwam of 1860 stood on this site later; the hotel burned 4 March 1851.

Andreas's 1884 engraving shows the hotel behind the separate log cabin and is now held on this hotel's Images tab. The main and side-range roof shapes and the left gable details remain under review against this retrospective picture. It does not establish every feature's exact condition on 1 July 1835, a historical viewing position, or literal paint colours.

lodging.note: The town model puts an inn or tavern at 9 people on an ordinary night and 35 when full, from the 1840 household tail (p90 and max of 964 Chicago households). This building takes the share of its class's total that its 159 m² of enclosed floor (79 m² × 2 storeys) is of the class's floor area.
lodging.replaceable_by: Any source that states this house's rooms, beds or lodgers on a dated day: an advertisement counting its rooms, a traveller's account of how many it slept, a licence return. A stated capacity retires the apportioned one outright.

occupancy.statement: 7 on this card against an ordinary night's 7 beds: 3 seated here from elsewhere in the layer, where no source gives them a roof, 4 drawn against the order book's lodging buckets for beds that were standing empty.
occupancy.keeper_owed: NOBODY KEEPS THIS HOUSE IN THIS DATASET. It is a documented building and no source this project holds names its keeper on 1 July 1835. A reconstructed proprietor is not written into a documented house: that is a research question, not a draw.

source_document.name: Sauganash Hotel

grade.why: Pictured: 3 of the pictures on the Images tab show it.

documented_range.note: Wau-Bun, describing 1831: 'a house just completed by Mark Beaubien.' Destroyed by fire 4 March 1851. The 1838 rename to Chicago Hotel and the 1837 arrival of the Chicago Theatre Company in the dining room are changes of use, not of form, so they do not open a new phase.

source_document.change_note: Two-story frame block built onto the log core at the Lake and Market corner, 1831; the whole then known as the Sauganash Hotel, Chicago's first hotel.

placement.position_note: PLACED 2026-08-09. The corner is documented — chicagology and the Chicago Landmark record both put the Sauganash at the south-east corner of Lake and Market — but the COORDINATE is inferred, so the tag follows the weaker half. Method: Market Street is today's N Wacker Drive and Lake Street is unchanged, an equivalence the research dossier states and the georeference independently corroborates, since the 1834 plats warped onto the modern street centrelines at 17.5 m RMS. The modern intersection centre was read from OpenStreetMap (EPSG:26916 E 447161.9, N 4637285.4) and the footprint origin offset 12.2 m east and 20.2 m south of it: half of an 80 ft platted street to reach the kerb, and the footprint's own 8 m depth so the building's north face sits on the Lake Street frontage of a south-east corner lot. Working uncertainty about 20 m, which is the georeference's, not an additional guess. Facade bearing 0 (north, onto Lake Street): the sources say it faced the forks to the north-west, so the true bearing is likely nearer 315, but the plat lot lines are orthogonal and a corner building fronting Lake is the defensible reading until better evidence appears.
placement.symbolic_location: South-east corner of Lake Street and Market Street (today Lake St and N Wacker Dr).

footprint.note: THE TWO-MASS PLAN, AND THE 12 x 8 m PLACEHOLDER IS RETIRED (T-0626, spending T-0617's reading). THE FRONTAGE IS DERIVED AND THE DEPTH IS NOT, and the block is graded at the weaker of the two. FRONTAGE 9.92 m: Braunhold's engraving draws five bays on the street face and rectified against that face's own vanishing point the five are EQUAL to 2.4 % (tools/measure_sauganash_plate.py, bay_rhythm.rectified_gaps 0.997 / 1.011 / 1.020 / 0.972). The bay measures 1.984 m at the plate's stated scale datum — a standing adult at 1.70 m, hat included, the two men on the walk reading 147 and 143 px — so five bays are 9.92 m. THE DATUM'S BIAS IS SMALL AND BOUNDED, which is what makes this a measurement rather than a floor: the men stand a pace forward of the wall, and the plate's own focal length puts them 43.0 m from the station (f 3664.7 px on a 145 px figure of 1.70 m), so a pace is 2.7 %. The frontage is therefore 9.9-10.2 m and 12 m IS REFUTED rather than merely unsupported. The value taken is the measured 9.92 and is not fudged up into the correction. What does still move it is the 1.70 m datum itself: at 1.60 m the frontage reads 9.3 m and at 1.80 m 10.5 m. DEPTH 8.0 m IS UNCHANGED AND IS STILL A RECONSTRUCTION. One plate gives no depth (docs/RESEARCH/sauganash_image_accuracy.md row 11), so nothing has measured it; it is held at the placeholder's own figure deliberately, because the placement above offsets this origin by the footprint's own 8 m depth to stand the north face on the Lake Street frontage, and moving a number with no evidence behind it would move the building. THE SECOND MASS IS NOT IN THIS POLYGON, on the precedent green_tree_tavern's rear ell set: an attached wing is the archetype's, sized by this phase's own form attributes (cross_wing, cross_wing_depth_m, cross_wing_end), and the polygon is the main block's plan. The one lead this note used to carry is still open: Andreas vol. 1 p. 106 ('Eagle Exchange'), not yet read at page-image level, and the individual building rectangle on Hathaway 1834. NOTE ON WHAT THIS TAG MEANS: conjectural here is about SIZE, not about existence or character. That the building was a two-storey white frame block is documented (Wau-Bun); how big it was is measured off one retrospective sheet and no better. The renderer therefore does NOT dither the massing on account of this tag — see generators/archetypes/frame_tavern.py — and the dimensional uncertainty is carried in the sidecar instead.

paint.note: Wau-Bun: 'a pretentious white two-story building, with bright-blue wooden shutters.' Painted white siding was itself remarkable at Wolf Point in 1831 — the description exists because the building stood out.

shutters.note: Wau-Bun, same sentence. The single most distinctive documented visual feature of the building. Wau-Bun gives the COLOUR and nothing else about the leaves; since T-0092 the leaf construction is carried by shutter_type — a far weaker, single-view claim graded on its own.

shutter_type.note: THE WEAKEST OF THE THREE VIEWS' CLAIMS, AND CARDED AS SUCH — IMAGE 10 ONLY. The Trowbridge drawing (image 10 of data/sources/assets/owner_brief_2026_08_18/README.md) is the one view that resolves the leaves at all, and it draws 'louvred shutters on the sash'; the Petford watercolour and the Braunhold engraving read at no such grain and can neither agree nor disagree, and Wau-Bun's sentence gives only the colour. One tier-5 retrospective drawing may still drive a fenestration detail as inferred — the same rule that admitted the Green Tree's plate-read chimney placement — but nothing corroborates this one, so the slats carry this attribute's confidence in the mesh rather than the attested colour's. T-0075 LANDED THE IDENTIFICATION ON 2026-08-22: image 10 is W. E. S. Trowbridge's drawing of the Sauganash, held as `trowbridge_sauganash_hotel`, and this row cites it instead of a README path. The plate was retrieved and read to confirm the louvres before the record was written. The citation changes nothing about the grade — a tier-5 retrospective still may not drive a coordinate, and this one is still uncorroborated by the other two views. Slat count and pitch are the archetype's numbers: docs/LIBERTIES.md L154.

construction.note: Balloon framing was developed in Chicago in 1832-33 and became the dominant local method. This building predates that by a year, so balloon framing is the LESS likely reading: a braced frame built onto a log core is more probable for 1831. Flagged for correction — the value is retained only until the framing question is researched, and it should probably become braced_frame. Do not treat this as settled.

cladding.note: Implied by 'white' painted finish on a frame building; clapboard is the standard cladding for the type and period. Not directly attested.

wall_height_m.note: RETAGGED 2026-08-09 from conjectural to inferred. No figure is attested for this building, but two full storeys at typical period floor heights is derivation from typology and construction practice, which is what 'inferred' means — the previous tag said 'no evidence' while this very note gave the reasoning. 5.5 m is about 18 ft: two 8 ft storeys plus floor structure and a low sill course. The DIMENSION remains uncertain; what is inferred is that it falls in this range, not that it is exactly 5.5 m.

roof_type.note: RETAGGED 2026-08-09 from conjectural to inferred, for the same reason as wall_height_m: gable is the near-universal roof form for frame buildings of this type, period and region, and both retrospective depictions show one. Typological derivation is 'inferred'. Not separately attested for this building by any period source.

gallery.note: REVISED 2026-08-09 after examining the images directly. No period source attests a gallery or porch either way, but the two surviving retrospective depictions both show the building WITHOUT one: the F. Braunhold engraving in Andreas (1884) and panel 14 of the Kurz and Allison sheet (1893) each show a plain two-story clapboard block with a modest entrance and no veranda. Caveat on independence — the Kurz and Allison panel closely follows the Andreas composition and is probably derived from it, so these are not two witnesses so much as one witness and a copy. 'No gallery' is therefore better attested than 'gallery' without being documented. See docs/RESEARCH/sauganash_hotel.md.

log_wing.note: RETIRED 2026-09-04 (T-0626), BECAUSE IT WAS THE SAME BUILDING DRAWN TWICE. This attribute stood a one-storey log wing FORWARD of the frame block's street face at its left third, and the owner reported exactly that from the dev preview: 'there is an extra log structure you have in front'. Two things are wrong with it and they are different. WHERE: all three views put the log annex at the END of the composition, beside the tall wing, and the main block's street face is unobstructed in every one of them. WHOSE: the annex is not this record's to draw. drloih_beaubien captions the very engraving this project measures — 'The Sauganash Hotel. The log cabin on the left was Chicago's first drugstore' — and that cabin is data/structures/philo_carpenter_log_shop.json, the 16 x 20 ft log building Andreas puts on Lake Street near the river, held here since 2026-08-11 and already sited hard against this block's EAST face on the same Lake Street frontage. So the annex stands in the scene, at the end, beside the wing; it simply stood there twice. The value is false rather than deleted so that the claim, its sources and its grade stay legible. The 1829 cabin's survival is not withdrawn — it is carried on the log_1829 phase below, which is that same building, and on the shop's own record.

roof_pitch_deg.note: T-3055 WORKING PICTURE REFINEMENT, NOT A MEASURED HISTORICAL PITCH. Keeping the existing9.92x8m footprint,5.5m walls and exact provisional camera,25.2degrees puts the withheld near ridge apex near(636.5,350.1) against an approximate source pick(648,350), replacing the old38degree projection near(636.5,231.4). fenestration.note: No period source describes the window arrangement. A regular five-bay elevation with a centred entrance is the standard disposition for a building of this size and type, and both retrospective depictions show regular bays. The COUNT and SPACING are inference; that it was regularly fenestrated is safe. MEASURED 2026-09-04 (T-0626, spending T-0617): the scheme this attribute has carried all along is the one the plate draws, and it is no longer typological inference. Braunhold's street face detects five openings in the upper storey and five in the ground storey, with the door the MIDDLE of the five — the darkest opening on the ground storey at ink 0.494, and nothing else on the sheet is inked like an open door onto an unlit room. The five are EQUAL: drawn gaps of 169.2, 161.1, 153.0 and 137.5 px are a 20.4 % spread that reads as an irregular rhythm and is not one, rectifying to 0.997, 1.011, 1.020 and 0.972 against the face's own vanishing point. The GRADE does not move — one sheet, tier 5, its two companions copies of it — and neither does the geometry, which already drew this. What changes is that the row now rests on a measurement: docs/RESEARCH/sauganash_image_accuracy.md rows 1-4.

entrance_frontispiece.note: A SMALL FLAT-HOODED FRONTISPIECE ON THE MAIN BLOCK'S FRONT DOOR. Both street views of the 2026-08-18 owner brief draw it (data/sources/assets/owner_brief_2026_08_18/README.md): the Petford 1831 watercolour puts 'a small flat-hooded entrance frontispiece/porch on the front door' (image 8), and the Braunhold engraving in Andreas draws 'the clapboard block's wide entrance surround' (image 9). This is a door SURROUND, not the veranda the gallery attribute records as absent — the same views that show the frontispiece show no gallery, so the two claims agree rather than conflict. Tier-5 retrospective views may drive form as inferred and never a dimension: the hood and pilaster sizes are the archetype's numbers, claimed at docs/LIBERTIES.md L154. The brief's binaries are not yet committed, so the citation is the README until T-0075 lands identifications.

chimneys.note: Both retrospective depictions show two. A tavern of this size needed multiple fireplaces. Not attested by a period source; the number is inference. The stacks' material is carried by chimney_material since T-0092.

chimney_material.note: BRICK STACKS, AND THE COLOUR RESTS ON ONE VIEW: the Petford 1831 watercolour (image 8 of data/sources/assets/owner_brief_2026_08_18/README.md) colours both chimneys brick-red over the white clapboard — the only coloured witness to this building — and the engraved views draw masonry stacks without being able to say of what. Brick is also the plausible reading on its own terms: a hotel raised in 1831 at the settlement's centre, when brick was reaching Chicago in trade, and no period text describes the stacks either way. A single tier-5 view may drive a material as inferred; the brief's binaries are not yet committed, so the citation is the README until T-0075 lands identifications.

roof_colour.note: THE PETFORD VIEW'S TONE, AND ONLY ITS: the 1831 watercolour (image 8 of data/sources/assets/owner_brief_2026_08_18/README.md) gives the shingle roof a dark green/moss colour — weathered shingles gone green, or the painter's reading of them — and the engravings, being monochrome, can neither agree nor disagree. A single tier-5 watercolour may drive a material tone as inferred; the exact colour value is the archetype's, claimed at docs/LIBERTIES.md L154. The brief's binaries are not yet committed, so the citation is the README until T-0075 lands identifications.

siding_exposure_m.note: INVENTED WITHIN A STOCK SET, NOT DERIVED. No source states the exposed face of any Chicago building's siding. The value is one of four period mill sidings — 4.5, 5, 5.5 or 6 in to the weather; this record wears 4.5 in — dealt by tools/deal_siding_stock.py: keyed to the phase's construction season, because buildings sided from the same season's shipments of St Joseph sawn lumber tend toward one stock, then advanced so no frame building within 60 m shares this one's. The separation is the surface variety T-0049 reconstructs, not a claim about 1835. docs/LIBERTIES.md L148 owns the invention.

cross_wing.note: THE SECOND TWO-STOREY MASS, AND THE PLATE PROVES IT BY ARITHMETIC. The owner reported it missing on 2026-09-03 from the dev preview: 'i think there is a structure missing but you have it on the front and they have it on the rear in pictures, and it looks like the full height of the main building and similar design as the main building appears to be almost the same size, it connects from the back and side in the images.' T-0617 measured the near apex at (648, 350) with one line running out of it at image slope -0.318 and one at +0.095, and called the right-hand one a ridge on the strength of the asymmetry alone. T-0626 finished the sum. Project each line onto the vertical through the vanishing point of the plane it lies in — the plate gives both horizontal vanishing points and its own focal length, recovered from their orthogonality — and BOTH come out horizontal in the world: 1.35 deg and 0.11 deg, where a 38 deg rake in the same plane would have been DRAWN at image slope -1.99 against the -0.318 measured. So they are two RIDGES meeting at one apex, not a ridge and a rake, and the mass the owner reported is on the sheet as a measurement rather than as an impression. tools/sauganash_apex_lines.py is that arithmetic and tools/check.sh gates on it. THE SHARED APEX IS ALSO WHAT SIZES THE WING: two gable ridges of one wall height and one pitch meet at a point only when they span the same width, so the wing's span is this block's own depth and the archetype refuses to build it at any other. GRADE. One sheet — Braunhold's. The Petford watercolour and the Trowbridge drawing are the same composition from the same station, so they copy it rather than corroborate it (docs/RESEARCH/sauganash_image_accuracy.md section 1), and a tier-5 retrospective that passes its own perspective test may be read for PROPORTION and never for a coordinate. CITED ON BRAUNHOLD ALONE. The Petford and Trowbridge views were dropped from this row on 2026-09-04 for the reason the reading itself gives: they are the same composition from the same station, so listing them would dress a copy as a corroboration. The earlier separate rights concern is now superseded by verified 1902 publication, but the dependence argument still applies: a later copy is not independent corroboration.

The lot decides. This phase's placement stands the block's WEST face on Market Street's east kerb line at a 0 m setback, so a wing at the west end would stand in Market Street. It goes at the EAST end — x_max in the archetype's local frame — which is also the end the log annex already stands against: data/structures/philo_carpenter_log_shop.json is set hard on this block's east face, by the same elimination and stated there since 2026-08-11. The plat equivalence, the kerb line and the 0 m setback are all this phase's own position block, which carries its sources; repeating them here would claim a second, independent standing this row does not have.
