function.note:
A tavern from 1829 and a hotel from 1831; the social centre of the settlement in the target window. Chicago's first billiard table in a public house stood here.

THE HOUSE IS OPEN, AND FRESHLY DONE UP, THREE WEEKS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE. Reviewing the town's public houses against Detroit's new American Hotel, the Chicago Democrat of 10 June 1835, page 2 column 5, claim chicago_democrat_1835_06_10#c001, reports that 'The Sauganash has been re[paired,] fitted up and furnished with neatness and [taste,] and so far as it goes, will[, we have no doubt,] be found just the thing'. That is the only dated statement of this building's CONDITION the corpus holds, and it bears on how the scene should read it: on 1835-07-01 the Sauganash is a working, recently refitted public house and not the shabby survivor its 1829 log origins invite. 'so far as it goes' is the editor's qualification and it means small — his complaint in the same paragraph is that no establishment in Chicago is 'sufficiently extensive'. The refit is recorded here rather than in the form block below because nothing in it names a fabric, a storey or a colour, and inventing one from 'fitted up' is exactly the supply this project refuses.

occupants.note: The Beaubiens owned it until 1834; the hotel chronology gives 'Davis (1835)' as operator, possibly the John Davis running the Steamboat Hotel on North Water Street. Mark Beaubien himself had moved on by the scene date — he built the Exchange Coffee House at Lake and Wells in 1834. The 1835 proprietor is a lead, not a settled fact.

built.note: Wau-Bun, describing 1831: 'a house just completed by Mark Beaubien.'

PRIOR RESEARCH RECORD:
MILESTONE 0 REFERENCE RECORD. Two things are documented and vivid — the white two-story frame and the bright-blue shutters, both from Wau-Bun — and two things are unknown: the building's dimensions and whether it had a gallery. That combination is exactly why the per-attribute confidence model exists, and this record is deliberately the first one in the dataset. See docs/RESEARCH/sauganash_hotel.md for the source conflicts and the reasoning behind each reading. The Wigwam of 1860 stood on this site later; the hotel burned 4 March 1851.

Andreas's 1884 engraving shows the hotel behind the separate log cabin and is now held on this hotel's Images tab. The main and side-range roof shapes and the left gable details remain under review against this retrospective picture. It does not establish every feature's exact condition on 1 July 1835, a historical viewing position, or literal paint colours.

document.name: Beaubien's log cabin, beside the Sauganash
aka: the log shop beside the Sauganash

grade.why: Pictured: 3 of the pictures on the Images tab show it.

documented_range.note: THE END OF THIS RANGE IS THE WEAKEST CLAIM IN THIS RECORD AND IT IS WEAKER THAN HOGAN'S, WHICH IS SAYING SOMETHING. What is attested: Philo Carpenter reached Chicago on 18 July 1832 and opened the town's first drug store in a log building 16 x 20 ft on Lake Street near the river. The range opens on the day he arrived because no source gives the shop a build date and he cannot have opened it earlier. THE PROBLEM IS WHAT HE DID NEXT. In the summer of 1833 Carpenter bought a lot on South Water Street between LaSalle and Wells and 'erected a small store' — carpenter_south_water_store in this dataset — and no source reached says what became of the log shop when he moved his trade into it. So this building is placed in a scene set two years after its proprietor built himself a better one, on nothing but the ordinary continuity argument that a standing building stands until something says otherwise. THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT IS SPECIFIC AND STRONG. Lake Street beside the Sauganash was the most valuable frontage at the forks; a 16 x 20 ft log shop is the smallest building in this dataset; and its one attested occupant demonstrably left it. A CONTEMPORARY DOCUMENT NARROWS NOTHING HERE. The Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 carries Carpenter's own advertisement, dated 22 November 1833, offering drugs, medicines, oils, paints and dye-stuffs and also dry groceries, glass and nails — proof that he was trading at Chicago sixteen months after arriving and nineteen months before the scene date, but it gives no address, so it cannot say WHICH of his two buildings he was trading from, and it must not be read as evidence that the log shop survived. GRADE: this record's existence at the scene date is the single most likely thing in this parcel to be wrong. If evidence turns up that the log shop came down or was moved before July 1835 it belongs in data/exclusions.json and this record leaves the scene.

document.change_note: Mark Beaubien's own log cabin — the Eagle Exchange of 1829 — standing on at the Lake and Market corner after the frame Sauganash was built onto it in 1831, and let from then on. Philo Carpenter opened Chicago's first drug store in it in the late summer of 1832 and 'soon' moved out; Beaubien let it next to John S. Wright; from September 1833 it held Eliza Chappel's school, which moved into the First Presbyterian Church in 1834. On 1835-07-01 all three uses are over and no source reached says what the room was doing, or names anyone in it.

placement.position_note: PLACED 2026-08-11, AND UNIQUELY IN THIS PARCEL IT IS PLACED AGAINST ANOTHER BUILDING RATHER THAN AGAINST A STREET. The sources give a relation, not an address: a log building on Lake Street near the river, 'immediately adjacent to the Sauganash's public bar' (docs/research/03-structures-north.md section 1), and since 2026-09-04 also drloih_beaubien's 'his original log cabin, adjacent to his Sauganash Tavern'. So this position is derived from data/structures/sauganash_hotel.json's own placement and inherits every uncertainty in it. MOVED 2.08 M WEST ON 2026-09-04 (T-0626), and only because the wall it is set against moved: the Sauganash's frame_1831 footprint stopped being a 12 x 8 m placeholder and became a measured 9.92 x 8 m block, so its east face came in from E 447186.1 to E 447184.02 and this shop came with it. Nothing here is a new claim about where the shop stood; it is the same claim re-derived from a corrected wall. THE SAUGANASH'S PLACEMENT, RESTATED SO THIS RECORD CAN BE RE-DERIVED: the Sauganash stands at the south-east corner of Lake and Market, its frame_1831 footprint origin at EPSG:26916 E 447174.1, N 4637265.2, 9.92 m wide and 8 m deep with a facade bearing of 0, so its north face is on the Lake Street frontage at N 4637273.2 and its east face at E 447184.02. THIS SHOP IS SET HARD AGAINST THAT EAST FACE, its own west wall on E 447184.02 and its north face on the same Lake Street frontage, which is what 'immediately adjacent' means and is why the two footprints touch. WHICH SIDE THE BAR WAS ON IS NOT ATTESTED and the east side is chosen by elimination: the Sauganash's west face stands on the Market Street frontage, so there is no room for a building there at all. THAT ELIMINATION NOW CARRIES A SECOND BUILDING TOO. Until 2026-09-04 this note read that the retrospective depictions put the surviving 1829 log wing on the hotel's LEFT FRONT, 'which is the Market side', and the hotel's own record drew a log wing there. Both were wrong in the same way: the views are drawn from a station, not from a compass, and a log annex on the Market side would stand in Market Street exactly as a shop would. The annex at the left of every view IS THIS BUILDING — drloih_beaubien captions the engraving 'The log cabin on the left was Chicago's first drugstore' — so the hotel's log_wing attribute is retired and the hotel's second, TALL wing takes the same east end, standing back off the rear beside this cabin. WORKING UNCERTAINTY ABOUT 20 M, the georeference's residual (data/datum.json, 17.5 m RMS), carried in from the Sauganash rather than added to; the 2.08 m correction above is inside it many times over and changes nothing about what this record knows. Facade bearing 0, north onto Lake Street, and the 20 ft dimension is set along the street with the 16 ft as the depth — the same convention hogan_store's record argues for and, like it, an inference rather than evidence. Turning the shop through 90 degrees would make it a 16 ft frontage 20 ft deep, and nothing decides.
placement.symbolic_location: Lake Street near the river, on the south side, immediately east of and against the Sauganash Hotel — the source says immediately adjacent to the Sauganash's public bar.

footprint.note: THE SECOND BUILDING FOOTPRINT IN THIS DATASET THAT IS EVIDENCE RATHER THAN A PLACEHOLDER, after Hogan's store. Andreas gives the size: a 16 x 20 ft log building. 16 x 20 ft is 4.877 x 6.096 m, recorded converted with the original figures stated, per data/datum.json's units rule. WHAT IS DOCUMENTED IS THE SIZE AND NOT THE PLAN: '16 x 20' is a rectangle in any reading and this polygon is that rectangle, but nothing attests a door, a counter, or that the building was exactly rectangular rather than a rectangle with a shed on the back. WHICH AXIS RUNS ALONG THE STREET IS NOT IN THE SOURCE either; it is decided by the facade bearing and argued in the position note, where it belongs. This is the smallest building in the dataset — 30 square metres, a single pen — and that is worth reading twice: Chicago's first drug store was a room.

construction.note: Andreas: a log building. No source describes the corner treatment, the chinking or whether any of it was sided; the archetype builds hewn log, which is the commonest construction at the forks in 1832 and what the source names.

stories.note: Not stated. A 16 x 20 ft single-pen log building is single-storey by type, and a two-storey building on that plan would be a tower. Inference from the documented dimensions, which is as close to derivation from evidence as this dataset's storey counts get.

wall_height_m.note: No figure is attested. 2.5 m is about 8 ft: one storey of hewn log wall at typical period course counts, plus a sill. The same reading and the same number this project gives Hogan's store and the Walker meeting house.

roof_type.note: Not attested. Gable is the near-universal roof form for log construction of this type, period and region. A shed roof leaning on the Sauganash's east wall is the one plausible alternative — 'immediately adjacent' could describe a lean-to — and it is recorded here rather than built, because nothing in the sources describes the junction between the two buildings.

function.note: THREE DOCUMENTED FORMER USES AND NO CURRENT ONE, AND THE RECORD MUST NOT INVENT A FOURTH. Corrected 2026-09-04 (T-0626) on the owner's explicit instruction; before that this field read 'drug_store' and the record was titled Philo Carpenter's Log Drug Store, which named a trade that had left the building three years before the scene date. THE CHAIN, in order, from drloih_beaubien: 'In the late summer of 1832, he rented his original log cabin, adjacent to his Sauganash Tavern, to the newly arrived Philo Carpenter for use as - Chicago's 1st - drugstore. An ardent enemy of alcohol, Carpenter soon moved out. Mark next rented the space to John S. Wright, and in 1833, the cabin became a school under Eliza Chappel's direction.' drloih_chappell dates and ends the school independently: it opened in September 1833 in 'a small log house formerly used as a store', and 'in 1834, the school was moved into the First Presbyterian Church'. Andreas corroborates the first link from a different direction, giving Carpenter's drug store a size and a street — 16 x 20 ft of log on Lake Street near the river. SO ON 1 JULY 1835 IT IS NEITHER A DRUG STORE NOR A SCHOOL. Carpenter's own advertisement in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 proves the trade was still his that month but carries no address, and he had built his South Water Street store the previous summer, so it cannot put the trade in this room. A dwelling is the likeliest use in a town where housing was scarce, and that is a guess, so the value says 'unattested' instead of making it — the same construction data/structures/chappel_infant_school.json and data/structures/watkins_school_house.json already use. THE TAG FOLLOWS THE WEAKEST HALF: the uses are documented, their ENDING before the scene date is documented, and what is inferred is that the building stood empty or in some unrecorded use rather than gone.

occupants.value: no occupant attested at the scene date; Philo Carpenter 1832, John S. Wright 1832-33, Eliza Chappel's school 1833-34
occupants.note: THE THREE TENANTS ARE NAMED AND THEIR TENANCIES ARE OVER, which is the whole point of this field and is why it is written with end dates rather than carried forward. Mark Beaubien owned the cabin and let it: Carpenter from the late summer of 1832 and 'soon' out, John S. Wright next, then Eliza Chappel's school from September 1833 until it moved into the First Presbyterian Church in 1834. NO SOURCE REACHED NAMES ANYONE IN THIS BUILDING IN 1835. The school's mistress is a person this dataset already holds: data/residents/households/hh_chappel_eliza_mir, where she appears under her married name — drloih_chappell dates the marriage to the Rev. Jeremiah Porter to 15 June 1835, sixteen days before the scene date, and by then she had left both this room and, shortly, the town. THE SITE OF HER FIRST SCHOOL IS AN OPEN CONFLICT AND IS NOT RESOLVED HERE. drloih_beaubien puts it in this cabin at Lake and Market. Andreas puts a log school-house west of State Street between South Water and Lake, which this dataset holds separately as data/structures/chappel_infant_school.json. drloih_chappell's own opening line says 'roughly at Lake and Clark', which is where the school MOVED in 1834. Three sitings from three readings of two unfootnoted pages and one compiled secondary, and nothing reached decides between them — so both records stand, both say so, and neither is promoted. What is NOT in doubt on any of the three is that the school had left wherever it started by 1834.

citations.citation: "Eliza Emily Chappell, the First Chicago Teacher Paid by Public Funds in 1833." Digital Research Library of Illinois History Journal, 19 January 2018.
what_it_supplies: THE SCHOOL'S FIRST ROOM AND THE DATE IT LEFT IT: "Chappell arrived in Chicago in June 1833 with the prospects of opening a school by September. The school was established in a small log house formerly used as a store... In 1834, the school was moved into the First Presbyterian Church in Fort Dearborn, on the southwest corner of Lake and Clark Streets."
A LOG HOUSE FORMERLY USED AS A STORE is the phrase that joins to drloih_beaubien's cabin, let first to Philo Carpenter for a drug store and then, in 1833, to Chappel's school.

The school as it was kept: 25 students who furnished their own chairs, no desks, some paddling canoes across the river to it, and "maps, a globe, scriptural texts and hymn books, and illustrations of geometry and astronomy" for teaching tools.

No way past the three-way conflict it sits in: Andreas puts a log school-house west of State Street between South Water and Lake (data/structures/chappel_infant_school.json), drloih_beaubien puts the first room in Beaubien's cabin at Lake and Market, and this page carries the third reading.
No footnote, no dimension, and no description of the room itself.

document.research_note: A RARE COMBINATION AND THE REASON THIS RECORD IS WORTH HAVING: THE FOOTPRINT IS EVIDENCE AND THE EXISTENCE IS NOT. Andreas gives the dimensions — 16 x 20 ft, log, Lake Street near the river — which makes this only the second footprint in the dataset that is not a placeholder, after Hogan's store. Everything about whether it was still there on 1835-07-01 is argued on documented_range and it is argued against: Carpenter built himself a store on South Water in the summer of 1833 and nothing follows the log shop after that. THE CONTEMPORARY ADVERTISEMENT DOES NOT RESCUE IT. The Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 carries Carpenter's own notice and it is genuine primary evidence that he was trading — but it carries no address, it is nineteen months before the scene date, and by then he already had two premises. THE CONTINUITY ARGUMENT GOT STRONGER ON 2026-09-04 AND THE TRADE ARGUMENT GOT WEAKER, and they are different arguments. Stronger: drloih_beaubien and drloih_chappell put two further tenants in this room after Carpenter — John S. Wright, then Eliza Chappel's school until 1834 — so the building is now attested standing and IN USE eight months later than any source previously reached, and the 'a standing building stands until something says otherwise' argument runs over a much shorter gap. Weaker: the drug store is no longer even a candidate for the scene date, and the record's name, function and occupants now say so (T-0626). THIS IS ALSO MARK BEAUBIEN'S ORIGINAL CABIN, which is the identification that changed the most here. drloih_beaubien captions the engraving this project measures — 'The Sauganash Hotel. The log cabin on the left was Chicago's first drugstore' — so the log annex in all three views IS this building, and until 2026-09-04 the Sauganash's own record drew a second one as an attached log wing in FRONT of its street face. That wing is retired and this record is the annex. The hotel's log_1829 phase is the same fabric earlier, and its footprint has been reconciled to the 16 x 20 ft carried here; the two records are not merged and sauganash_hotel.json states why. THE POSITION IS DERIVED FROM ANOTHER RECORD, which is a first here: the source gives a relation and not an address, so this shop is set hard against the Sauganash's east wall and inherits that building's placement and its uncertainty — including, on 2026-09-04, a 2.08 m move west when that wall was measured. The two footprints touch, deliberately. WHAT WOULD SETTLE ANY OF IT: the individual building rectangles on Hathaway 1834 or Wright 1834 at the Lake and Market corner, which would show whether one building or two stood on that frontage; the Chicago Democrat for 1834-35, where an address in one of Carpenter's later advertisements would place his trade; a footnote anywhere for the Beaubien or Chappel pages; or a source that decides between this cabin and the State Street log house as the site of Chappel's first school. See docs/RESEARCH/philo_carpenter_log_shop.md.

documented_range.note: THE END OF THIS RANGE IS THE WEAKEST CLAIM IN THIS RECORD AND IT IS WEAKER THAN HOGAN'S, WHICH IS SAYING SOMETHING. What is attested: Philo Carpenter reached Chicago on 18 July 1832 and opened the town's first drug store in a log building 16 x 20 ft on Lake Street near the river. The range opens on the day he arrived because no source gives the shop a build date and he cannot have opened it earlier. THE PROBLEM IS WHAT HE DID NEXT. In the summer of 1833 Carpenter bought a lot on South Water Street between LaSalle and Wells and 'erected a small store' — carpenter_south_water_store in this dataset — and no source reached says what became of the log shop when he moved his trade into it. So this building is placed in a scene set two years after its proprietor built himself a better one, on nothing but the ordinary continuity argument that a standing building stands until something says otherwise. THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT IS SPECIFIC AND STRONG. Lake Street beside the Sauganash was the most valuable frontage at the forks; a 16 x 20 ft log shop is the smallest building in this dataset; and its one attested occupant demonstrably left it. A CONTEMPORARY DOCUMENT NARROWS NOTHING HERE. The Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 carries Carpenter's own advertisement, dated 22 November 1833, offering drugs, medicines, oils, paints and dye-stuffs and also dry groceries, glass and nails — proof that he was trading at Chicago sixteen months after arriving and nineteen months before the scene date, but it gives no address, so it cannot say WHICH of his two buildings he was trading from, and it must not be read as evidence that the log shop survived. GRADE: this record's existence at the scene date is the single most likely thing in this parcel to be wrong. If evidence turns up that the log shop came down or was moved before July 1835 it belongs in data/exclusions.json and this record leaves the scene.

source_document.change_note: Mark Beaubien's own log cabin — the Eagle Exchange of 1829 — standing on at the Lake and Market corner after the frame Sauganash was built onto it in 1831, and let from then on. Philo Carpenter opened Chicago's first drug store in it in the late summer of 1832 and 'soon' moved out; Beaubien let it next to John S. Wright; from September 1833 it held Eliza Chappel's school, which moved into the First Presbyterian Church in 1834. On 1835-07-01 all three uses are over and no source reached says what the room was doing, or names anyone in it.

placement.position_note: PLACED 2026-08-11, AND UNIQUELY IN THIS PARCEL IT IS PLACED AGAINST ANOTHER BUILDING RATHER THAN AGAINST A STREET. The sources give a relation, not an address: a log building on Lake Street near the river, 'immediately adjacent to the Sauganash's public bar' (docs/research/03-structures-north.md section 1), and since 2026-09-04 also drloih_beaubien's 'his original log cabin, adjacent to his Sauganash Tavern'. So this position is derived from data/structures/sauganash_hotel.json's own placement and inherits every uncertainty in it. MOVED 2.08 M WEST ON 2026-09-04 (T-0626), and only because the wall it is set against moved: the Sauganash's frame_1831 footprint stopped being a 12 x 8 m placeholder and became a measured 9.92 x 8 m block, so its east face came in from E 447186.1 to E 447184.02 and this shop came with it. Nothing here is a new claim about where the shop stood; it is the same claim re-derived from a corrected wall. THE SAUGANASH'S PLACEMENT, RESTATED SO THIS RECORD CAN BE RE-DERIVED: the Sauganash stands at the south-east corner of Lake and Market, its frame_1831 footprint origin at EPSG:26916 E 447174.1, N 4637265.2, 9.92 m wide and 8 m deep with a facade bearing of 0, so its north face is on the Lake Street frontage at N 4637273.2 and its east face at E 447184.02. THIS SHOP IS SET HARD AGAINST THAT EAST FACE, its own west wall on E 447184.02 and its north face on the same Lake Street frontage, which is what 'immediately adjacent' means and is why the two footprints touch. WHICH SIDE THE BAR WAS ON IS NOT ATTESTED and the east side is chosen by elimination: the Sauganash's west face stands on the Market Street frontage, so there is no room for a building there at all. THAT ELIMINATION NOW CARRIES A SECOND BUILDING TOO. Until 2026-09-04 this note read that the retrospective depictions put the surviving 1829 log wing on the hotel's LEFT FRONT, 'which is the Market side', and the hotel's own record drew a log wing there. Both were wrong in the same way: the views are drawn from a station, not from a compass, and a log annex on the Market side would stand in Market Street exactly as a shop would. The annex at the left of every view IS THIS BUILDING — drloih_beaubien captions the engraving 'The log cabin on the left was Chicago's first drugstore' — so the hotel's log_wing attribute is retired and the hotel's second, TALL wing takes the same east end, standing back off the rear beside this cabin. WORKING UNCERTAINTY ABOUT 20 M, the georeference's residual (data/datum.json, 17.5 m RMS), carried in from the Sauganash rather than added to; the 2.08 m correction above is inside it many times over and changes nothing about what this record knows. Facade bearing 0, north onto Lake Street, and the 20 ft dimension is set along the street with the 16 ft as the depth — the same convention hogan_store's record argues for and, like it, an inference rather than evidence. Turning the shop through 90 degrees would make it a 16 ft frontage 20 ft deep, and nothing decides.
placement.symbolic_location: Lake Street near the river, on the south side, immediately east of and against the Sauganash Hotel — the source says immediately adjacent to the Sauganash's public bar.

footprint.note: THE SECOND BUILDING FOOTPRINT IN THIS DATASET THAT IS EVIDENCE RATHER THAN A PLACEHOLDER, after Hogan's store. Andreas gives the size: a 16 x 20 ft log building. 16 x 20 ft is 4.877 x 6.096 m, recorded converted with the original figures stated, per data/datum.json's units rule. WHAT IS DOCUMENTED IS THE SIZE AND NOT THE PLAN: '16 x 20' is a rectangle in any reading and this polygon is that rectangle, but nothing attests a door, a counter, or that the building was exactly rectangular rather than a rectangle with a shed on the back. WHICH AXIS RUNS ALONG THE STREET IS NOT IN THE SOURCE either; it is decided by the facade bearing and argued in the position note, where it belongs. This is the smallest building in the dataset — 30 square metres, a single pen — and that is worth reading twice: Chicago's first drug store was a room.

construction.note: Andreas: a log building. No source describes the corner treatment, the chinking or whether any of it was sided; the archetype builds hewn log, which is the commonest construction at the forks in 1832 and what the source names.

stories.note: Not stated. A 16 x 20 ft single-pen log building is single-storey by type, and a two-storey building on that plan would be a tower. Inference from the documented dimensions, which is as close to derivation from evidence as this dataset's storey counts get.

wall_height_m.note: No figure is attested. 2.5 m is about 8 ft: one storey of hewn log wall at typical period course counts, plus a sill. The same reading and the same number this project gives Hogan's store and the Walker meeting house.

roof_type.note: Not attested. Gable is the near-universal roof form for log construction of this type, period and region. A shed roof leaning on the Sauganash's east wall is the one plausible alternative — 'immediately adjacent' could describe a lean-to — and it is recorded here rather than built, because nothing in the sources describes the junction between the two buildings.

The finite native trial and direct visual review accepted the lower roof as closer to the depiction. function.note: THREE DOCUMENTED FORMER USES AND NO CURRENT ONE, AND THE RECORD MUST NOT INVENT A FOURTH. Corrected 2026-09-04 (T-0626) on the owner's explicit instruction; before that this field read 'drug_store' and the record was titled Philo Carpenter's Log Drug Store, which named a trade that had left the building three years before the scene date. THE CHAIN, in order, from drloih_beaubien: 'In the late summer of 1832, he rented his original log cabin, adjacent to his Sauganash Tavern, to the newly arrived Philo Carpenter for use as - Chicago's 1st - drugstore. An ardent enemy of alcohol, Carpenter soon moved out. Mark next rented the space to John S. Wright, and in 1833, the cabin became a school under Eliza Chappel's direction.' drloih_chappell dates and ends the school independently: it opened in September 1833 in 'a small log house formerly used as a store', and 'in 1834, the school was moved into the First Presbyterian Church'. Andreas corroborates the first link from a different direction, giving Carpenter's drug store a size and a street — 16 x 20 ft of log on Lake Street near the river. SO ON 1 JULY 1835 IT IS NEITHER A DRUG STORE NOR A SCHOOL. Carpenter's own advertisement in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 proves the trade was still his that month but carries no address, and he had built his South Water Street store the previous summer, so it cannot put the trade in this room. A dwelling is the likeliest use in a town where housing was scarce, and that is a guess, so the value says 'unattested' instead of making it — the same construction data/structures/chappel_infant_school.json and data/structures/watkins_school_house.json already use. THE TAG FOLLOWS THE WEAKEST HALF: the uses are documented, their ENDING before the scene date is documented, and what is inferred is that the building stood empty or in some unrecorded use rather than gone.

occupants.value: no occupant attested at the scene date; Philo Carpenter 1832, John S. Wright 1832-33, Eliza Chappel's school 1833-34
occupants.note: THE THREE TENANTS ARE NAMED AND THEIR TENANCIES ARE OVER, which is the whole point of this field and is why it is written with end dates rather than carried forward. Mark Beaubien owned the cabin and let it: Carpenter from the late summer of 1832 and 'soon' out, John S. Wright next, then Eliza Chappel's school from September 1833 until it moved into the First Presbyterian Church in 1834. NO SOURCE REACHED NAMES ANYONE IN THIS BUILDING IN 1835. The school's mistress is a person this dataset already holds: data/residents/households/hh_chappel_eliza_mir, where she appears under her married name — drloih_chappell dates the marriage to the Rev. Jeremiah Porter to 15 June 1835, sixteen days before the scene date, and by then she had left both this room and, shortly, the town. THE SITE OF HER FIRST SCHOOL IS AN OPEN CONFLICT AND IS NOT RESOLVED HERE. drloih_beaubien puts it in this cabin at Lake and Market. Andreas puts a log school-house west of State Street between South Water and Lake, which this dataset holds separately as data/structures/chappel_infant_school.json. drloih_chappell's own opening line says 'roughly at Lake and Clark', which is where the school MOVED in 1834. Three sitings from three readings of two unfootnoted pages and one compiled secondary, and nothing reached decides between them — so both records stand, both say so, and neither is promoted. What is NOT in doubt on any of the three is that the school had left wherever it started by 1834.

source_document.research_note: A RARE COMBINATION AND THE REASON THIS RECORD IS WORTH HAVING: THE FOOTPRINT IS EVIDENCE AND THE EXISTENCE IS NOT. Andreas gives the dimensions — 16 x 20 ft, log, Lake Street near the river — which makes this only the second footprint in the dataset that is not a placeholder, after Hogan's store. Everything about whether it was still there on 1835-07-01 is argued on documented_range and it is argued against: Carpenter built himself a store on South Water in the summer of 1833 and nothing follows the log shop after that. THE CONTEMPORARY ADVERTISEMENT DOES NOT RESCUE IT. The Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 carries Carpenter's own notice and it is genuine primary evidence that he was trading — but it carries no address, it is nineteen months before the scene date, and by then he already had two premises. THE CONTINUITY ARGUMENT GOT STRONGER ON 2026-09-04 AND THE TRADE ARGUMENT GOT WEAKER, and they are different arguments. Stronger: drloih_beaubien and drloih_chappell put two further tenants in this room after Carpenter — John S. Wright, then Eliza Chappel's school until 1834 — so the building is now attested standing and IN USE eight months later than any source previously reached, and the 'a standing building stands until something says otherwise' argument runs over a much shorter gap. Weaker: the drug store is no longer even a candidate for the scene date, and the record's name, function and occupants now say so (T-0626). THIS IS ALSO MARK BEAUBIEN'S ORIGINAL CABIN, which is the identification that changed the most here. drloih_beaubien captions the engraving this project measures — 'The Sauganash Hotel. The log cabin on the left was Chicago's first drugstore' — so the log annex in all three views IS this building, and until 2026-09-04 the Sauganash's own record drew a second one as an attached log wing in FRONT of its street face. That wing is retired and this record is the annex. The hotel's log_1829 phase is the same fabric earlier, and its footprint has been reconciled to the 16 x 20 ft carried here; the two records are not merged and sauganash_hotel.json states why. THE POSITION IS DERIVED FROM ANOTHER RECORD, which is a first here: the source gives a relation and not an address, so this shop is set hard against the Sauganash's east wall and inherits that building's placement and its uncertainty — including, on 2026-09-04, a 2.08 m move west when that wall was measured. The two footprints touch, deliberately. WHAT WOULD SETTLE ANY OF IT: the individual building rectangles on Hathaway 1834 or Wright 1834 at the Lake and Market corner, which would show whether one building or two stood on that frontage; the Chicago Democrat for 1834-35, where an address in one of Carpenter's later advertisements would place his trade; a footnote anywhere for the Beaubien or Chappel pages; or a source that decides between this cabin and the State Street log house as the site of Chappel's first school. See docs/RESEARCH/philo_carpenter_log_shop.md.

documented_range.note: THE 1835 GROUNDBREAKING IS NOT ANDREAS. The separately admitted June 10 Chicago Democrat notice establishes an active project before the scene; modern compilations are not the only evidence for this site. chicagology_prefire112 prints an Andreas passage and then two uncredited editorial paragraphs with no typographic break. ANDREAS says: 'Chicago did, however, have a really grand hotel as early as 1835; this was the Lake House, located on the corners of Kinzie, Rush and Michigan streets, fronting on the latter. This hotel, which was built of brick, was three stories and a basement in height, was elegantly furnished throughout, and cost its owners nearly $100,000. ... The hotel was completed and thrown open to the public in the autumn of 1836.' He gives NO groundbreaking. THE UNCREDITED PARAGRAPH says: 'ground was broken in 1835, and opened in the fall of 1836'. The same paragraph drops Andreas's basement and gives $90,000 against his nearly $100,000, so it is demonstrably not a faithful restatement of the text it sits under, and 'ground broken in 1835' must not be cited as Andreas. data/exclusions.json's lake_house_finished entry sources the 1835 groundbreaking to drloih_hotels, which is a second unfootnoted compilation saying the same thing; two compilations agreeing is not two witnesses. SO: from 1835-01-01, the first day the attested year permits and not a date anybody gives. TO 1836-12-31, a bound at the end of the year the hotel opened - Andreas's 'autumn of 1836' ends this construction state and no source dates the day. WHAT NARROWS THE MIDDLE, and it is the best anchor this record has: J. D. Bonnell, in a letter to the Chicago Times dated 15 March 1876 and quoted by Andreas, describes arriving in Chicago and walking the town the next morning - 'Passing east, toward the mouth of the river, was THE LAKE HOUSE IN COURSE OF CONSTRUCTION, east of which was the residence of Dr. Kimball.' Bonnell dates his arrival in the same letter to 'August 25, 1835'. That is eight weeks after the scene date and it is an eyewitness saying the building was visibly going up and not finished. HIS DATE IS NOT CLEAN AND THE CONFLICT IS RECORDED RATHER THAN HIDDEN: the letter opens 'My first entry into the city of Chicago was forty years ago, August 25, 1835' - forty years before 1876 is 1836 - and Andreas's own lead-in says Bonnell 'came to Chicago in 1837'. The 1837 reading is ruled out by the letter's own content, since the Lake House was open by the autumn of 1836; between 1835 and 1836 the letter's explicit date is preferred. Harriet Martineau, quoted by Andreas from June 1836, still calls it 'a new hotel then building', which is consistent with either. CURRENT EVIDENCE CORRECTION: the earlier ONLY THING wording is superseded by the separate Chicago Democrat notice of 10 June 1835, page 2 column 5, already cited under function. Its transcription-mediated reading supports an active named project before the scene but no precise groundbreaking day, roof or construction stage. function.note:
The building's purpose is documented and its completion date is documented, and between them they make the scene-date function a construction site rather than a hotel. Andreas: 'Chicago did, however, have a really grand hotel as early as 1835; this was the Lake House ... The hotel was completed and thrown open to the public in the autumn of 1836, Jacob Russel, of Middleton, Conn., assuming control of its management.' The men behind it are documented too and are worth carrying because they are the town's commercial leadership rather than innkeepers: Gurdon S. Hubbard, General David S. Hunter, John H. Kinzie, Dr W. B. Egan and Major James B. Campbell - 'the men whose enterprise led them into building a house which for those days was far in advance of the needs of the town'.

AND THE SCENE-YEAR PRESS DATES THE SITE, WHICH ANDREAS DOES NOT. 'There is [a] new house building in Kinzie's addition [to be] named we understand, the "Lake Hous[e]."' — the Chicago Democrat of 10 June 1835, page 2 column 5, claim chicago_democrat_1835_06_10#c001, the same paragraph that reports the Sauganash freshly refitted. Both halves are load-bearing. IT IS A BUILDING SITE three weeks before the scene date, north of the main branch, which is what makes hotel_under_construction an attested function at 1835-07-01 rather than a back-projection from the 1836 opening. AND ITS NAME IS STILL SECOND-HAND — 'we understand' — so on the scene date the town has an unfinished building that people are calling the Lake House and not a hotel with a sign. The same paragraph contains an editorial proposal for a house 'about double the size of that latter' near the centre of Lake Street on this side of the river. The comparison expresses a desired relative hotel size; it supplies no measured dimensions or July construction stage and does not establish the Lake House's rank among existing buildings. The proposal is not an existing-house observation and does not prove that the suggested site was vacant.

Fergus's 1876 recollection of the 1839 hotel is included here only for later establishment identity and the conflicting Rush/North Water address, not as evidence of the July 1835 construction stage, position or dimensions. Its Hotels entry was directly checked at the printed page; the existing contemporary project notice remains the evidence for work before the scene date.

THE MARGIN IS 51 m: this footprint stands that far inside the tract's nearest boundary, which is more than twice the working horizontal uncertainty of anything traced off the 1834 sheets (about 20 m), so the assignment survives the error the construction carries. WHAT THIS ROW CLAIMS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It claims that the tract the Illinois State Archives' land-sale register describes contains this structure's committed position — the patent for this ground was ENTERED by this man on this date. document.research_note:
The Lake House was building before this scene: the Chicago Democrat of 10 June 1835 reports a new house building in Kinzie's Addition, understood to be named Lake House. The held newspaper reading is transcription-mediated, with bracketed supplies; no original facsimile was newly read. Andreas says the completed hotel was brick, three storeys and a basement, and opened in autumn 1836.

LIBERTIES: No source dates its precise progress on 1 July. The scene chooses an incomplete, roofless working lift: stepped brick walls, seven selected work bays, open apertures and two internal timber stages. The 24 × 15 m extent, four-metre maximum, masonry thickness, smaller lifts and staging are reconstructed. Brick, timber and footing stone beside it are the existing reconstructed yard layer. No below-grade cellar is depicted. The open shell represents one bounded choice within the retained zero-to-two-storey uncertainty; that uncertainty does not require an empty site.

THE PICTURE SHOWS A LATER STATE: kellogg_blanchard_1856_old_fort_lake_house is the public-domain 1856 Kellogg/Blanchard print, misleadingly stored under an 1830 filename. Its labelled Lake House has a completed roof, cupola and three window rows in a scene of about 1836–1849. It is linked as later context and does not attest this July stage. No completed-state geometric match or July picture is claimed. The duplicate planning image is the same composition; Milwaukee's Lake House is a different hotel. The source page also carries an about-1860 completed-hotel photograph and an 1869 map, plus two later text-ad/menu images; none depicts July progress.

SITING: The existing reconstructed position follows Andreas's Kinzie/Rush/Michigan account and the north-side Michigan Street reading (today Hubbard), with about twenty metres of survey uncertainty and an unresolved side-of-Rush choice. Fergus's 1839 address recalled in 1876 instead prints Rush and North Water. The source page's 1869 map places the later hotel west of Rush, contradicting the existing reconstructed east-side choice. This is recorded as a later mapped-state conflict, without asserting that the later plan measures this July worksite. That later conflict does not justify moving the July site to the modern Wrigley gloss. Bonnell's date conflict remains recorded in the research dossier. The source/date coverage and finite worksite acceptance are in docs/RESEARCH/lake-house-completion-20261110/README.md.

documented_range.note: THE 1835 GROUNDBREAKING IS NOT ANDREAS. The separately admitted June 10 Chicago Democrat notice establishes an active project before the scene; modern compilations are not the only evidence for this site. chicagology_prefire112 prints an Andreas passage and then two uncredited editorial paragraphs with no typographic break. ANDREAS says: 'Chicago did, however, have a really grand hotel as early as 1835; this was the Lake House, located on the corners of Kinzie, Rush and Michigan streets, fronting on the latter. This hotel, which was built of brick, was three stories and a basement in height, was elegantly furnished throughout, and cost its owners nearly $100,000. ... The hotel was completed and thrown open to the public in the autumn of 1836.' He gives NO groundbreaking. THE UNCREDITED PARAGRAPH says: 'ground was broken in 1835, and opened in the fall of 1836'. The same paragraph drops Andreas's basement and gives $90,000 against his nearly $100,000, so it is demonstrably not a faithful restatement of the text it sits under, and 'ground broken in 1835' must not be cited as Andreas. data/exclusions.json's lake_house_finished entry sources the 1835 groundbreaking to drloih_hotels, which is a second unfootnoted compilation saying the same thing; two compilations agreeing is not two witnesses. SO: from 1835-01-01, the first day the attested year permits and not a date anybody gives. TO 1836-12-31, a bound at the end of the year the hotel opened - Andreas's 'autumn of 1836' ends this construction state and no source dates the day. WHAT NARROWS THE MIDDLE, and it is the best anchor this record has: J. D. Bonnell, in a letter to the Chicago Times dated 15 March 1876 and quoted by Andreas, describes arriving in Chicago and walking the town the next morning - 'Passing east, toward the mouth of the river, was THE LAKE HOUSE IN COURSE OF CONSTRUCTION, east of which was the residence of Dr. Kimball.' Bonnell dates his arrival in the same letter to 'August 25, 1835'. That is eight weeks after the scene date and it is an eyewitness saying the building was visibly going up and not finished. HIS DATE IS NOT CLEAN AND THE CONFLICT IS RECORDED RATHER THAN HIDDEN: the letter opens 'My first entry into the city of Chicago was forty years ago, August 25, 1835' - forty years before 1876 is 1836 - and Andreas's own lead-in says Bonnell 'came to Chicago in 1837'. The 1837 reading is ruled out by the letter's own content, since the Lake House was open by the autumn of 1836; between 1835 and 1836 the letter's explicit date is preferred. Harriet Martineau, quoted by Andreas from June 1836, still calls it 'a new hotel then building', which is consistent with either. Seven selected work bays have real unglazed openings and only the first three have their brickwork bridged above reconstructed timber lintels; a broad rear break admits material. Two short timber working stages stand inside the shell. Bay count, wall thickness, lift heights, apertures, staging stock and placement are reconstructed working choices, not features traced from the later print. The existing external brick, timber and footing-stone piles remain separately declared in the yard layer. No excavation or below-grade interior is represented. L-lake-house-worksite-2379.

function.note:
The building's purpose is documented and its completion date is documented, and between them they make the scene-date function a construction site rather than a hotel. Andreas: 'Chicago did, however, have a really grand hotel as early as 1835; this was the Lake House ... The hotel was completed and thrown open to the public in the autumn of 1836, Jacob Russel, of Middleton, Conn., assuming control of its management.' The men behind it are documented too and are worth carrying because they are the town's commercial leadership rather than innkeepers: Gurdon S. Hubbard, General David S. Hunter, John H. Kinzie, Dr W. B. Egan and Major James B. Campbell - 'the men whose enterprise led them into building a house which for those days was far in advance of the needs of the town'.

AND THE SCENE-YEAR PRESS DATES THE SITE, WHICH ANDREAS DOES NOT. 'There is [a] new house building in Kinzie's addition [to be] named we understand, the "Lake Hous[e]."' — the Chicago Democrat of 10 June 1835, page 2 column 5, claim chicago_democrat_1835_06_10#c001, the same paragraph that reports the Sauganash freshly refitted. Both halves are load-bearing. IT IS A BUILDING SITE three weeks before the scene date, north of the main branch, which is what makes hotel_under_construction an attested function at 1835-07-01 rather than a back-projection from the 1836 opening. AND ITS NAME IS STILL SECOND-HAND — 'we understand' — so on the scene date the town has an unfinished building that people are calling the Lake House and not a hotel with a sign. The same paragraph contains an editorial proposal for a house 'about double the size of that latter' near the centre of Lake Street on this side of the river. The comparison expresses a desired relative hotel size; it supplies no measured dimensions or July construction stage and does not establish the Lake House's rank among existing buildings. The proposal is not an existing-house observation and does not prove that the suggested site was vacant.

Fergus's 1876 recollection of the 1839 hotel is included here only for later establishment identity and the conflicting Rush/North Water address, not as evidence of the July 1835 construction stage, position or dimensions. Its Hotels entry was directly checked at the printed page; the existing contemporary project notice remains the evidence for work before the scene date.

land_owner.value: The ground was entered by Robert A Kenzie, 7 May 1831
land_owner.note: KINZIE'S ADDITION. The north fraction of section 10 is the section north of the river, which is why the register prints 102.29 acres and not a quarter's 160. It is resolved as the section's own grid box clipped to the committed north bank of the main stem (`e1834_harbor_cut/shoreline.geojson`), so no boundary here is authored. The two rows the register carries for it — one plain, one with the school-section marker — are the same entry printed twice. THE REGISTER SPELLS THE PURCHASER MORE THAN ONE WAY for this same tract — Robert A Kenzie; Robert A Kinzie — and the spellings are carried rather than merged, which is the land_sales crosswalk's standing rule: tract agreement is where two spellings MIGHT be one man and is never proof that they are. THE MARGIN IS 51 m: this footprint stands that far inside the tract's nearest boundary, which is more than twice the working horizontal uncertainty of anything traced off the 1834 sheets (about 20 m), so the assignment survives the error the construction carries. WHAT THIS ROW CLAIMS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It claims that the tract the Illinois State Archives' land-sale register describes contains this structure's committed position — the patent for this ground was ENTERED by this man on this date. It does not claim he still held the ground on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it: a sale is a transaction, and the register's only column about residence names a county. THE SECTION LINES ARE CONSTRUCTED, NOT TRACED (L219): the grid is carried from the single PLSS corner at State & Madison, on the plat's own east-west bearing, in nominal one-mile squares.

source_document.research_note:
The Lake House was building before this scene: the Chicago Democrat of 10 June 1835 reports a new house building in Kinzie's Addition, understood to be named Lake House. The held newspaper reading is transcription-mediated, with bracketed supplies; no original facsimile was newly read. Andreas says the completed hotel was brick, three storeys and a basement, and opened in autumn 1836.

LIBERTIES: No source dates its precise progress on 1 July. The scene chooses an incomplete, roofless working lift: stepped brick walls, seven selected work bays, open apertures and two internal timber stages. The 24 × 15 m extent, four-metre maximum, masonry thickness, smaller lifts and staging are reconstructed. Brick, timber and footing stone beside it are the existing reconstructed yard layer. No below-grade cellar is depicted. The open shell represents one bounded choice within the retained zero-to-two-storey uncertainty; that uncertainty does not require an empty site.

THE PICTURE SHOWS A LATER STATE: kellogg_blanchard_1856_old_fort_lake_house is the public-domain 1856 Kellogg/Blanchard print, misleadingly stored under an 1830 filename. Its labelled Lake House has a completed roof, cupola and three window rows in a scene of about 1836–1849. It is linked as later context and does not attest this July stage. No completed-state geometric match or July picture is claimed. The duplicate planning image is the same composition; Milwaukee's Lake House is a different hotel. The source page also carries an about-1860 completed-hotel photograph and an 1869 map, plus two later text-ad/menu images; none depicts July progress.

SITING: The existing reconstructed position follows Andreas's Kinzie/Rush/Michigan account and the north-side Michigan Street reading (today Hubbard), with about twenty metres of survey uncertainty and an unresolved side-of-Rush choice. Fergus's 1839 address recalled in 1876 instead prints Rush and North Water. The source page's 1869 map places the later hotel west of Rush, contradicting the existing reconstructed east-side choice. This is recorded as a later mapped-state conflict, without asserting that the later plan measures this July worksite. That later conflict does not justify moving the July site to the modern Wrigley gloss. Bonnell's date conflict remains recorded in the research dossier. The source/date coverage and finite worksite acceptance are in docs/RESEARCH/lake-house-completion-20261110/README.md.

liberty.text:
final compact Agency-House form
DECISION
Reconstruct the compact centre, subordinate wings and two rear tails, preserving the existing text-supported partial lower clapboarding. The text supplies a compact centre, two wings, two rear tails and partial clapboarding. The keyed retrospective illustration supplies a dominant front gable, receding ridge, subordinate side gable, three front marks and one visible roof stack. Its few pixels are not metric evidence. Replace the prior13×9m trial with a9×4.5m reconstruction: centre5×3.5m, two2×2m wings recessed1m, and two1.5×1m rear tails. Wing eaves are2.0m; centre/tails retain2.6m. Parallel35° gables and unseen rear junctions are choices. One0.80m square stack 35 percent along the main ridge, head5.05m, replaces the unsupported two exterior wing stacks. It is a visible-count proxy, not proof that hidden flues never existed. Retain the1.30m board band and all three front marks with unchanged relative set-out/depth. Position and rotation values remain unchanged; no survey or terrain is fitted. The canonical illustrative camera uses five approximate front points at1.009px coordinate RMS, with about2px reading uncertainty, fixed800px focal and1.60m eye. This chooses a pose family, not a recovered historical viewing location; diagnostic only withholds From-this-spot navigation. Monochrome tone does not attest paint; paper white is not whitewash evidence. The drawing depicts1831, was reproduced1881 with1857credit, and cannot establish unchangedJuly1835form. Actual native side-by-side acceptance belongs in its match record, not this liberty. Unpictured exact dimensions, rear forms, finish dates and survival are reconstructed within the already stated historical limits. The companion held unkeyed panorama the chicago fort dearborn 1831 2 image is also enrolled as waubun 1831, with a1.724px front fit and about2px point uncertainty. Its inventory Sarony/Wau-Bun attribution is qualified, and it is not independent evidence. Both actual native views must be reviewed; their lower-mark extents and minor roof proportion disagreement are within tolerance underT3153.
SOURCES
Kinzie, Juliette A. M. Wau-Bun: The 'Early Day' in the North-West, [Unresolved Beaubien-group identification, preferred working residence] “Fort…, Andreas, A. T. History of Chicago: From the Earliest Period to the Present Time.
HOW TO RESOLVE
A dimensioned contemporary plan or detailed, independently identified early view could replace the compact reconstruction and establish hidden roof junctions or the date of the partial siding. Current small retrospective depictions support bounded form rather than measured dimensions.

two gable levels and connector form (2026-11-10)
DECISION
Green Tree's current enclosed left annex is an evidence-bounded reconstruction, using the actually viewed public-domain Andreas1884 Green Tree plate and Kurz&Allison1893 panel11 ("THE GREEN TREE HOTEL." — wood engraving, in A. T. Andreas, History of Chicago…, Kurz & Allison. Chicago In Early Days, 1779-1857), with Trowbridge/Gale1902 as explicit counterevidence (The Green Tree Tavern in 1835 (published 1902)). Andreas and Kurz draw a low foreground gable and a separate higher rear gable; the previous constant-height turned range omitted that second silhouette. A raised rear section now supplies it. Its1.6m depth, 4.5m wall and37degree roof, the range's3.7m depth/1.7m front set-out, and the existing25degree plan turn are RECONSTRUCTED controls. The range's back corner stays put; the forward wall and its physical entrance advance together0.7m. The low connector falls away from the main block toward the foreground range, with working high/low edges3.0/2.25m. Existing clapboard stock continues over shed infill rather than leaving a flat proxy patch. The foreground upper-light sill drops3.1to2.7m with its existing0.65x0.70m section retained. None of these numbers is a metric measurement from a retrospective drawing, a surveyed plan, a dated alteration, an asserted interior or extra lodging capacity. The pictures may be dependent. Trowbridge's open wagon bay and different upper/attic openings, Gray's later side entrance and bilateral additions, and the held c1859 catalogue lead remain explicit. Those image-to-image and camera-fit conflicts are within tolerance underT3153 and prove no conversion year. The site file named1859 is an engraving showing later commercial shopfronts, lettering, awnings and a gas lamp, not an authenticated CHM ICHi040230 photograph; neither that held reproduction nor the unverified, check required museum lead supplies this geometry or a derived asset. The core footprint, world placement, source rights and source grades do not change. Genuine final native pictures and published app review supply acceptance; a source proposal or CPU diagnostic alone does not.
SOURCES
"THE GREEN TREE HOTEL." — wood engraving, in A. T. Andreas, History of Chicago…, Kurz & Allison. Chicago In Early Days, 1779-1857, The Green Tree Tavern in 1835 (published 1902).
HOW TO RESOLVE
An independently identified contemporary plan or detailed view could replace the chosen metric controls and settle the competing closed-shoulder and open-wagon-bay readings. The dependent retrospective images and later commercial views establish no July conversion date or recovered historical camera.

JAIL · OUTBUILDING

North-west corner of the court-house square

The autumn 1833 log jail remains the only documented county institutional building on 1 July 1835. The source-informed keeper house, enclosure and pitched core are included by explicit continuity reconstruction from Gale’s 1835-framed recollection and the detailed public-domain plate captioned 1836. Core eave 3.35 m and pitch 28 degrees replace the earlier low proxy; one upright gable light follows the depicted shape. Exact dimensions and continuity are reconstructed. The existing footprint, fabric, phase dates and reconstructed setback are retained, with no later courthouse or extra cell backdated and no new household.

bounded core form (2026-11-10)
DECISION
Log jail, phase log 1833, retains the documented 1833 log jail, existing reconstructed footprint/site and source dates. The detailed independently public-domain Gale/Trowbridge 1902 plate (captioned 1836) is selected for its taller log gable and one upright barred-looking gable light; Gale p51's 1835-framed recollection supplies the continuity context, not proof of every detail by 1 July. Eave 3.35 m, pitch 28°, east gable registration, 0.48 x 0.85 m light, three uprights, one crossbar, 55 mm framing and continued gable course relief are explicit reconstruction choices, not measured historical dimensions or structural/interior evidence. They replace the low 2.66 m/12° proxy while keeping keeper/enclosure/the footprint file and phase dates unchanged. Andreas 1884's hip/pyramidal cap, different domestic elevation and absent core flues are retained as contradictory retrospective appearance, within tolerance under later work; no second cell or post-July courthouse is invented to reconcile the pictures. No geometry is derived from the separately rights-held UCR/1947 copies. The reframed northeast Gale eye is diagnostic only, with unchanged full source pixels, and supplies no historic “From this spot” action. Acceptance requires actual refreshed native comparisons and published street review; this Liberty does not claim a match by itself.
SOURCES
Cook County’s First Jail as it was in 1836 (published 1902), Andreas, A. T. History of Chicago: From the Earliest Period to the Present Time.
HOW TO RESOLVE
A contemporary dated view or measured plan could replace the selected core profile and opening controls and establish its exact July 1835 appearance. The 1836 retrospective caption and contradictory Andreas roof remain explicit; no date or second cell is invented to reconcile them.

Two-story frame block built onto the log core at the Lake and Market corner, 1831; the whole then known as the Sauganash Hotel, Chicago's first hotel.

HOW MANY SLEPT HERE

7 on an ordinary night · 35 when full RECONSTRUCTED

The town model puts an inn or tavern at 9 people on an ordinary night and 35 when full, from the 1840 household tail (p90 and max of 964 Chicago households). This building takes the share of its class's total that its 159 m² of enclosed floor (79 m² × 2 storeys) is of the class's floor area. liberty.text:
Sauganash pictured masonry heads
DECISION
Andreas/Braunhold's retrospective 1884 engraving draws two slender brick stacks with projecting masonry heads. The earlier two ridge-end shafts had plain tops, which omitted that visible form. Keep their 0.60 m square sections and 0.60 m end insets; select complete tops 0.75 m above the ridge, of which the last 0.12 m is a square cap projecting 0.06 m on every side (0.72 m overall). The shaft ends at ridge +0.63 m. All of those dimensions are reconstructed working choices, bounded by the drawn slender, capped profile; none is a historical metre, counted brick course or dated July-1835 alteration read from the plate. Source: "THE SAUGANASH HOTEL." — wood engraving, in A. T. Andreas, History of Chicago…. These choices use the opt-in ridge end chimney head; absence preserves the existing kit exactly. The retained compound roof has an 8 m reconstructed rear range, following the owner's earlier “almost the same size” reading. The plate supplies no independent wing length or historical station. A separate analytical Hotel wall-corner fit changes the near roof apex by about 74 px vertically with geometry unchanged, so the broad left-wing exposure and small far-gable visibility in the retained Shop-fit camera do not establish another physical dimension. Those source/camera exposure differences are adjudicated under the camera-fit tolerance; no plan, phase date, paint or placement is moved to erase them.
SOURCES
"THE SAUGANASH HOTEL." — wood engraving, in A. T. Andreas, History of Chicago…, the verified public-domain retrospective plate, used for relative shape only.
HOW TO RESOLVE
A contemporary detailed stack view or measured record could replace the bounded head sections. The retained diagnostic camera and retrospective line weight do not independently determine historic metres, brick courses or a July fitting date.

HOTEL, UNDER CONSTRUCTION · FORT STRUCTURE

North side of the river in Kinzie's Addition

On 1 July 1835 this is an active hotel-building project, attested by the 10 June notice. Its particular stage is reconstructed: an uneven, roofless brick lift with open work bays and two internal timber stages, on the existing 24 × 15 m plan at a 4 m maximum. No completed-hotel roof, cupola, glazing, sign or accommodation is backdated from the later image.

Inferred. Known from maps or written records; no picture of it has been found.

Dates not recorded

hotel, under construction

none
OWNER OF THE GROUND
The ground was entered by Robert A Kenzie, 7 May 1831
HOW MANY SLEPT HERE

The record's own function says this building was still going up on 1835-07-01. A house that was not open held nobody, and giving it a capacity would put beds in a building site.

liberty.text:
finish a bounded July worksite, without backdating the later hotel
DECISION
Lake House (under construction) uses the default-off construction site builder: thick, open brick walls with uneven lifts, seven selected work bays, only three bridged openings supported by reconstructed timber lintels, a broad rear material-access break and two interior timber working stages. All pieces stay within the existing 24 × 15 m footprint and four-metre maximum. The existing nine external material piles stay on their independently declared yard layer.
EVIDENCE AND BOUNDS
The held Chicago Democrat 10 June 1835 p.2 col.5 notice attests an active project before 1 July, not its measured progress; the reading is transcription-mediated, with bracketed supplies, and no original facsimile was newly read. Andreas's later completed brick hotel, three storeys and a basement, and autumn 1836 opening bound a substantial unfinished project. The exact July lift is a chosen reconstruction within the retained zero-to-two-storey range. The 0.46 m masonry, chosen seven-bay rhythm, individual apertures, incomplete lintels, lower lifts and 1.65 m stage decks/stock/positions are all invented within those bounds. No source counts or measures them. No cellar excavation, below-grade interior, accommodation or completed-hotel roof/cupola/glazing/sign is represented. The prior position and its uncertainty are retained; no later address or retrospective print relocates it.
PICTURE SCOPE
The original Chicago picture is the 1856 Kellogg/Blanchard print, showing the completed ca.1836–1849 hotel. Its planning copy is byte-identical. All four Lake House illustrations embedded in the live Chicagology source page were also read: the about-1860 completed-hotel photograph, the 1869 mapped hotel and two later text-ad/menu composites. None depicts July progress; no asset is derived from that check required site. The 1869 map places the later hotel west of Rush, contradicting the existing reconstructed east-side choice; that later-state conflict is recorded without tracing it into July coordinates. Milwaukee's Lake House is a different building. The completed print remains credited later context and is ineligible to prescribe July construction progress. No empty matches verdict is created. Any image-gate exception for the original piece of work must name this wrong-date ruling. A measured contemporary plan or dated progress picture could replace the reconstruction; missing exact numbers do not block building it at this row.
SOURCES
The Chicago Democrat. Vol. I, No. 1 (November 26, 1833) through Vol. II, No. 18…, Andreas, A. T. History of Chicago: From the Earliest Period to the Present Time.
HOW TO RESOLVE
A measured contemporary plan or dated July construction-progress view could replace the selected lifts, bays and staging. The completed ca.1836–1849 hotel picture remains later context, not evidence of the July worksite.
