placement.position_note: PLACED 2026-08-11. THE CORNER IS DOCUMENTED TWICE AND THE COORDINATE IS DERIVED, so the tag follows the weaker half — the rule the Sauganash and Green Tree placements use. Wau-Bun: 'It stood at what is now the southwest corner of Wolcott and N. Water Streets.' Andreas, independently: 'the agency-house on the north side of the river, near where now is the foot of North State Street', with his footnote citing Wau-Bun for the same corner. METHOD, in three steps. (1) Wolcott Street is today's N State Street; its modern centreline was read from OpenStreetMap through the Kinzie intersection (EPSG:26916 E 447899.73, N 4637671.53, local E +827.0, N +275.7) and carried south on the fitted bearing of the OSM centreline, giving E +830 at this northing and a west kerb 12.2 m west of it, half an 80 ft platted street. (2) North Water Street and the 1834 north bank were read off the Wright 1834 sheet at the project's own fitted affine (tools/wright_px.py, the same transform tools/rederive_datum.py checks the datum against): the north-bank block row's south line, which is North Water Street's north kerb, runs at local N +128 to +132 between E +624 and E +812, and the drawn north bank of the main stem runs at local N +98 over the same stretch. So the platted street occupies a strip about 30 m deep between the block row and the water. (3) The building's south face is set 15 m north of that bank line and its east face 4 m west of the State Street kerb. THE 15 M IS EVIDENCE, NOT A GUESS, AND IT IS SOFT: Andreas prints the testimony of Charles Jouett's daughter, Mrs. Susan M. Callis, who came here in 1816 and describes the agency house of that period as 'a log building of two large rooms, about twenty steps from the river bank, on the north side'. Twenty steps is 15-18 m. Two inferences ride on it — that a step is about three-quarters of a metre, and that the house Mrs. Callis describes is the one Wolcott finished, which Andreas's 'commenced during Judge Jouett's incumbency' supports and nobody states. WHAT THE SOUTH-WEST QUADRANT ACTUALLY IS: on the 1834 sheet there is no block in it. West of Wolcott the ground south of North Water Street is the riverbank itself, so the building sits on the bank between the platted street and the water rather than on a corner lot — which is what Wau-Bun describes from the other side: 'when, in the process of the town's improvement, a street was maliciously opened directly in the rear of the building, the whole establishment, with its comical little adjuncts, was a constant source of amusement to the passers-by.' The house predates the plat by a decade and the street was laid out behind it. That same sentence is the evidence for the facade bearing recorded here, 180, due south onto the river: the street opened at the REAR, so the front faced the water, which is also how the fort's people reached it — Wau-Bun has the intercourse between the garrison and the Agency House kept up by canoe. UNCERTAINTY: about 20 m from the georeference (data/datum.json records ~17.5 m RMS and calls 20 m the working figure), plus the reading of the 1834 sheet by eye at about 5 m, plus whatever 'twenty steps' is worth. Treat the across-bank axis as the softer one. A LARGER CAVEAT THAN ALL OF THOSE, AND IT IS DISCHARGED. When this note was written the building stood about 500 m east of the modelled terrain box and there was no modelled ground under it at all. The e1834_harbor_cut heightfield was extended east on 2026-08-11 to local E -320..+1700, N -400..+400 — docs/LIBERTIES.md L17 is revised to say so — and this position has stood on traced ground at about +1.35 m above the summer-1835 water surface ever since, which is why this phase carries no ground_contact declaration. Corrected 2026-08-22 under T-0010; walked in the real page by tools/measure_east_band.mjs.
placement.symbolic_location: South-west corner of Wolcott Street and North Water Street (today N State St and the north bank of the main stem), at the foot of State Street, north bank of the main stem east of the forks.

footprint.note: T-2374 final bounded reconstruction: the text-attested centre, two symmetrical wings and two rear tails occupy a 9 by 4.5 m envelope. The 5 m centre is retained; each former 4 m wing is narrowed to 2 m and its front recessed 1 m behind the central front. The central room is 3.5 m deep, and each 1.5 m wide rear tail runs 1 m back. These are choices within Wau-Bun's compact five-part composition and the small keyed panorama's dominant front gable and subordinate visible side gable, not measured historic dimensions or a survey. Room-coordinate rebasing keeps the polygon at local zero; position and rotation are unchanged. The central openings retain their earlier relative offsets, count, heights and depths. The generator builds the exact union, including re-entrant corners. The unseen wing, tails and continuation to July 1835 remain reconstructed. Supersedes the former 13 by 9 m trial; see L-cobweb-completion-2374.

construction.note: Wau-Bun: 'a substantial, compact little building of logs hewed and squared'. Andreas, recording David McKee's account of the north side when he arrived in 1823: 'All these houses were of logs — the agency-house being afterward clapboarded part way up.' Hewn and squared log is exactly what this archetype builds. The clapboarding is recorded separately under `cladding`, with its unknown extent and date kept explicit there.

cladding.note: 'the agency-house being afterward clapboarded part way up' — David McKee's recollection, printed by Andreas. This is an unusually specific finish for a building at this date and it is genuinely odd: siding taken part of the way up a log wall and no further, presumably to weather the lower courses. WHEN it was done is not stated beyond 'afterward', i.e. after 1823, so whether the boards were there on the scene date is not attested either. T-2374: the lower-wall reconstruction now represents this occurrence through compound_clapboard_height_m; its chosen half-wall extent, neutral finish and corner clearances are liberties; the original date qualification remains.

plan_composition.value: centre, two wings, two rear tails
plan_composition.note: Wau-Bun states centre, two wings and two rear tails, with symmetry from the front. The connected-room generator builds that composition; exact dimensions and roof arrangement are reconstructed from that text and the keyed panorama's dominant front gable and smaller visible side gable.

stories.note: Not attested. 'Compact little building' and 'two large rooms' both read as a single storey, and a building that grew by adding wings at the sides and tails at the rear is a building that could not grow upward — which is the argument. The counter-example is in the same book: the FIRST agency house, built beside old Fort Dearborn in 1803-4 on the south side, was 'a two-story log building, covered with split oak siding'. That is a different building and it is why this value is inference rather than type.

wall_height_m.note: No figure is attested. 2.6 m is about 8 ft 6 in: one storey of hewn-log wall at the course counts this project uses for the Miller house's log core, plus a sill. What is inferred is the range, not the centimetre.

roof_type.note: Wau-Bun describes an odd-shaped roof. The reconstruction carries five parallel gables: a dominant central roof, two recessed smaller wing roofs, and two narrow rear tail roofs. The keyed panorama supplies the dominant-front and visible-side-gable hierarchy; it cannot establish hidden valleys or rear roof forms. All exact junctions remain reconstructed.

roof_pitch_deg.note: Retained 35-degree reconstruction, bounded by the steep front gable in the retrospective panorama and log-roof practice. The tiny engraving and illustrative camera do not supply a measured pitch.

chimneys.note: The keyed panorama shows one small stack above the receding main ridge. One is adopted as a visible-count proxy, replacing the prior inferred pair of conspicuous exterior wing stacks. This is not proof that no hidden flue existed. Shaft section, position and continuation to July 1835 are reconstructed.

compound_parts.note: T-2374 final composition: five connected rooms exactly partition the reconstructed footprint. Parallel front-to-back gables replace the former transverse wing roofs: the 5 m centre has a dominant ridge, while each 2 by 2 m wing makes a subordinate gable recessed 1 m behind the front. Overlapping eaves meet at the room junctions; no valley flashing or hidden interior is claimed. The panorama bounds the hierarchy and visible side gable; Wau-Bun supplies two wings and two tails. Exact dimensions, depths, roof axes and unseen rear junctions remain reconstructed. The central and tail eaves retain 2.6 m; wing eaves are reconstructed at 2.0 m and all pitches retain 35 degrees.

compound_apertures.note: T-2374 FRONT APERTURE INCREMENT, AND THE COUNT IS THE ONLY THING THE PICTURE GIVES. The keyed panorama 'Fort Dearborn and Chicago in 1831', read here at full resolution on its Agency-House subject (chicago/reference/images/chicago/chicago_fort_dearborn_1831_1.jpg, sha256 624d8f1f52a75bf30653e8cbf37a388478b0ddf5a02f1fadf727cf2144b84c3f), draws the front gable with THREE dark marks: TWO upright ones standing on the ground line, and ONE small one high on the face at the head of the wall. The archetype's compound path states one opening per room, so that front could not be expressed at all and every data-only attempt at it was refused by the archetype's own validation; this attribute is the opt-in that lets one room state its own set, and it OVERRIDES the centre door that room's `front_opening` would otherwise put here, so the old opening does not survive among the new marks. WHAT IS READ AND WHAT IS INVENTED. Read from the picture: that there are two lower marks and one upper one; that the lower pair stand on the ground; and roughly where the three fall along the face, the lower pair in its left and middle leaving the right-hand stretch blank, the upper mark a little left of the apex. Invented: every dimension, every band, the depth and section of the recesses, and which of the two lower marks is the way in. The marks are a few pixels across a thirty-pixel gable in a retrospective engraving whose proportions are not this model's, so no fraction of them is carried across as a measurement: the coordinates here are set out from this record's own 5 m central wall and the rake of its own roof, inside the bounds the archetype validates. The face is drawn slightly oblique, which compresses its right-hand side, so even the arrangement is read with that caution. THE ENTRY ROLE IS A DESIGN INFERENCE AND NOT A READING. The picture does not say which mark was a door, or that either was. The right-hand one carries `kind: door` because it stands where this record's previous single centre door stood, so the town's entrance, apron and doorway clearance keep the ground they already held; the other is `kind: aperture`, which claims a hole and nothing else. No glazing, closure, interior, attic room, white paint or historic function is claimed by any of the three, and the white of the engraving's paper is not evidence of paint. T-2374 FINAL FORM SUPERSESSION: the three marks, their heights, widths, relative positions and recess depth are retained as the central room is rebased with the narrower wings. The final compound, roofs and stack have a canonical illustrative view in data/reference_views/cobweb_castle/kinzie_1831.json; its match record carries actual picture acceptance. The drawing remains retrospective 1831 context, not a measured survey or proof of an unchanged July 1835 condition. See L-cobweb-apertures-2374 and L-cobweb-completion-2374.

chimney_head_m.note: T-2374 retains the earlier reconstructed 5.05 m head, now on one central ridge stack. The retained 2.6 m eave, 5 m central span and 35-degree pitch put the central ridge about 4.526 m over grade, leaving about 0.524 m of head. The section 18 by-law clearance cited for T-3081 bounds this choice; it does not prove July 1835 compliance or a historical height. Placement and square section are separate reconstructed choices in compound_ridge_stacks.

compound_clapboard_height_m.note: T-2374 partial-clapboarding reconstruction: McKee's account printed by Andreas says the agency house was 'afterward clapboarded part way up'. The 1.30 m band is half the current inferred 2.6 m model wall, not a historical measurement. The exterior lower-wall fields use the existing neutral board finish and lap rhythm; upper logs and existing notched ends remain exposed, joined internal walls are not boarded, and all current apertures stay clear. Exact extent, corner treatment and the presence of this finish on 1 July 1835 are reconstructed choices; the account supplies no completion date. The 1.30 m band is retained in the final compound reconstruction; historical date uncertainty remains. Native and picture acceptance are recorded in the canonical reference view.

compound_ridge_stacks.note: T-2374: the panorama shows a small stack above the main roof rather than two large exterior wing-end stacks. Place one 0.80 m square shaft at 35 percent along room zero's ridge from the rear; its head uses the existing 5.05 m chimney_head_m. Every metric coordinate is reconstructed, bounded by the drawn roof stack and retained central roof. No hidden flue or historic construction section is claimed.

compound_eave_heights_m.note: T-2374: the visible subordinate side-gable eave is below the main eave in the keyed engraving. Choose 2.0 m for both symmetric wing walls, retaining the previous 2.6 m centre and rear tails. The approximately 0.6 m step is a bounded reconstruction, not a scale read from the drawing. All rooms retain the declared 1.30 m partial board band and exposed upper logs.

function.note: NOT AN OPERATING INDIAN AGENCY BUILDING AT THE SCENE DATE, most likely, and that is the fact this record has least evidence for. Andreas has it 'left unoccupied by the death of Dr. Wolcott' in 1830, then in the autumn of 1832 describes 'the old Indian agency-house in which Colonel Hamilton then resided' — Colonel R. J. Hamilton, the county's clerk and commissioner of school lands, living in it as a private house while the agency's business ran down through the 1833 treaty. Nothing reached says who was in it in July 1835 or what it was being used for, so the value records a residence and this record carries no occupants block rather than guessing at one.

stands_on_lot.note: MEASURED, NOT CLAIMED (T-1478). This record's committed footprint lies 100% on lot 1 of blk_kinzie_dearborn_north in the north_division_tier grid, which is where tools/plat_occupancy.py seats it: a building stands on the lot most of it is on, and only if it reaches the part of that lot a roof could use. THE LOT GRID WAS DRAWN AFTER THE BUILDING WAS PLACED (T-1194 and its children), so this is an observation about the ground under a committed coordinate and NOT an address — no source names this lot, `claims_lot` is false, and nothing about the record's placement, footprint, form or confidence moved to write it. The seat is graded at the weaker of the lot lines this block states (inferred) and the numeral on them (inferred), read from data/traces/vectors/north_division_tier_lots.json.

placement.position_note:
RE-SEATED 2026-10-22 ON THE OWNER'S REPORT (T-3029): 5.80 m WEST, the northing and bearing unchanged. The owner, in the 1835 scene: "green tree tavern in 1835 is sunken, it needs to be on the ground". It was: the renderer beds a building on the lowest ground under it, and the T-0141 seat below was measured on the footprint polygon alone, while the rear ell (form.rear_ell, built since T-0083 off the east gable) runs 4.5 m further down the bank, its far corner 1.54 m from the traced waterline. Bedded to the ell's foot, the inn stood 0.58 m under its own front door; bedded to its bounding box, as the renderer then did, 0.88 m. The rule is the T-0141 rule with the whole building in it: walked west a tenth of a metre at a time, this is the first seat at which every wall foot the mesh puts on the ground, ell included, meets the modelled ground within 0.10 m, the relief 95% of the 1835 town's structures stand on. Here it is 0.099 m, and the ell's far corner stands 4.59 m from the bank. The move is inside the 20 m working uncertainty below and argues nothing new about the corner: the source still puts the inn at Lake and West Water, and the bank still decides how close to it the inn can come. The paragraphs below are the T-0141 seat as it was measured, kept as the reading this one corrects.

MOVED 2026-09-24 ON THE OWNER'S RULING OF 2026-09-21 (T-0141): from the north-east corner of Lake and Canal to the north-east corner of Lake and West Water, 116.40 m east, measured between the old east face and the new one. The northing did not change at all. THE MOVE IS ARGUED FROM THE SOURCE AND NOT FROM A PICTURE'S FRAMING. DRLOIH's article on this tavern gives the corner as 'Lake and West Water Streets'; West Water was the street that ran along the west bank while Canal lay a full plat module further west, and the owner ruled that statement preferred over the same article's gloss 'now Canal Street'. The ship masts that read beside and beyond the inn rather than above its own roofline from the `green_tree` stand (T-0122, T-0140) are the SYMPTOM that sent somebody to look at the placement; they are not a reason to move a building.

WHAT THE OLD PLACEMENT WAS, because a committed building that moves without its previous reading surviving is a town quietly rewriting itself. PLACED 2026-08-09 at EPSG:26916 E 446937.4, N 4637299.6, facade bearing 270: the west face on Canal Street's east frontage and the south face on Lake's north frontage, each half an 80 ft platted street from the modern Lake-and-Canal intersection centre read from OpenStreetMap (E 446913.0, N 4637287.4). That reading rested on chicagology's 'Northeast Corner of Lake and Canal Streets' and on DRLOIH's own body text, 'the N.E. corner of what is now Lake and Canal Streets' — both name Canal in modern terms and one says 'what is now', which is why Canal was adopted at the time. The residual was recorded then and is the thing the ruling settled: modern Canal at Lake stands about 146 m back from the modern west-bank line, so the two readings are a full plat module apart. The check that would settle it from paper is still the lot geometry on Wright 1834 or Hathaway 1834, which nobody has read.

HOW THE NEW COORDINATE IS ARRIVED AT — two constraints, one of them recomputed by tools/validate.py. (1) NORTH OF LAKE, unchanged: the south face stands 12.192 m north of the Lake-and-Canal control's northing, half the 80 ft platted module, which is the `platted_corner` derivation below and keeps the building out of Lake's platted corridor. (2) THE RIVER END: the footprint's north-east corner stands 3.01 m from the 1834 traced west bank of the South Branch (data/terrain/epochs/e1834_harbor_cut/river.geojson) — 5.71 m measured due east at that corner's own northing — and the standoff is the MODELLED GROUND'S OWN LIMIT rather than a chosen setback. The bank falls away toward the water, and a 12.19 m sill plate cannot sit level across that fall: seated hard on the bank the footprint's perimeter stands 0.88 m off the terrain beneath it, which is a building arriving nowhere and would owe a liberty. Walked west a tenth of a metre at a time, the first seat whose whole perimeter comes within the walker's 0.35 m step-up of the modelled ground is this one, at 0.294 m, with the footprint dry at all 425 samples of a 24-by-16 grid over it. So the tavern comes forward to the bank as far as the committed ground carries it, which is what 'forward to the bank' can mean here. Facade bearing is UNCHANGED at 270, due west onto West Water: F. H. Taylor's 'The fornt was on Canal street and this side was on Lake' is a claim about the street the front faced, and on the ruling's reading that street is West Water; the long elevation still runs east-west along Lake, and John Gray's second entrance is still 'on the Lake street front about the middle of the long side'. Working uncertainty about 20 m, which is the georeference's and the traced bank's and not an additional guess.

WHAT THE MOVE DISPLACED, AND ON WHOSE RULE. The committed `west_water` centreline ran through this footprint. T-0768 carried the bank offset 37.12 m past the Wolf Point turn under a stated rule — carry it until the riverward corridor reaches a committed footprint that stands ACROSS the roadway rather than beside it, and cut the line there — and the Green Tree is now the first such footprint, its nearest corner 3.01 m from the bank and its furthest 15.90 m, so it stands across the roadway exactly as James Kinzie's house does. So the line is cut at local [-20.32, -98.49]: 22.53 m shorter, ending 2.30 m south of Lake's own north platted kerb. The owner's ruling anticipated a collision and named T-0251 to settle it — the loser re-seated on its own evidence before it is withdrawn — and this line's own evidence is the rule above. The cost is written where the street is, in data/streets/1835.json: Fergus 1839's 'W. Water st north of West Lake st' again attests a street this reconstruction gives no modelled length north of Lake. Nothing already placed was displaced; the nearest committed footprint is James Kinzie's house, whose nearest corner stands 9.14 m north-west of this one.

AND THE PLATE'S COMPOSITION NOW READS, which is what T-0122 asked for and what the old placement could not give. Plate "11" of the 2026-08-11 prefire views hangs ship masts over this tavern's roofline; from the old stand the nearest water on that bearing was 157 m out and a 14.5 m mast on a 1.1 m deck needed to be inside 83 m, so the masts read beside and beyond the inn instead. The schooner moored in the reach below the forks (data/boats/era_boats.json, boat_schooner_wolf_point_2, whose own note already called this reach 'the one open water on the Green Tree Tavern's own eastward sight line') now lies 29.16 m beyond the ridge. The ridge stands 7.98 m above the building's base — 5.0 m of wall and a 38 degree gable over a 7.62 m width — which is 8.96 m on the committed heightfield, and the masthead is 15.6 m above the water. A viewer has to stand at least 0.93 of the ridge-to-mast distance back from the ridge before the masthead clears it, so the `green_tree` stand moved with the building, to Lake Street's own south platted frontage 34.85 m from the ridge on the schooner's bearing (local [-44.11, -121.52], yaw 33.3). The masthead reads 1.44 m above the roofline there, and between 1.36 m and 1.52 m for an eye anywhere from 1.6 m to 1.8 m. From the old standoff — 12.2 m off the front wall — it still does not clear, and that is geometry rather than a placement question: an 8 m ridge seen from 12 m subtends more than a 15.6 m masthead seen from 41 m, wherever the building stands.
placement.symbolic_location: North-east corner of Lake Street and West Water Street, on the west bank of the South Branch; the long elevation on Lake, the front west onto West Water, the river end on the bank as far as the modelled ground carries it.

footprint.note:
DERIVED FROM THE ATTESTED INTERIOR, not invented and not measured. This is the only footprint in the parcel with a textual basis. The arithmetic, in the original units: guest chambers 'about 12x12' feet, so a depth of two 12 ft ranks plus board partitions gives about 25 ft = 7.62 m; a hall 'divided the house' with the entrance 'about the middle of the long side', so the length is two end blocks either side of a hall of about 8 ft, and each end block must hold a 12 ft room plus partitions, giving about 40 ft = 12.19 m. The bar-room occupied one whole end, which is consistent. WHAT IS ATTESTED IS THE MODULE, NOT THE COUNT: no source gives the building's overall length or width, and a plan with three rooms rather than two on one side would make it about 52 ft. Treat the length as plus or minus about 20 per cent and the depth as firmer. The polygon is the two-storey core only — the 'low one-story addition to the right, the same as on the left' that John Gray recalls is NOT included, because its size is unattested and its date is unknown. The c. 1859 photograph (chm_green_tree_1859) would settle the overall dimensions from the proportions of a known-height building; it has not been seen.

T-2376: this polygon remains the main block's dimension/coordinate reference. The separately reconstructed left connector and gabled range are described by form.enclosed_left_annex. Their exact resolved occupied polygons are carried separately to physical consumers; the open wagon bay is not silently filled by a bounding rectangle. This does not add an archival dimension or date to the core. This model-only preparation does not yet qualify additional occupied solids or navigation/ground consumers; the main-body footprint stays unchanged until the separate compound-consumer work is verified.

additional_polygons.note: Occupied ground of this reconstructed annex component; its exact resolved frame also builds the walls and door. The open yard bay is not a solid connecting polygon.
Occupied ground of this reconstructed annex component; its exact resolved frame also builds the walls and door. The open yard bay is not a solid connecting polygon.

stories.note: 'a two-story frame building' (DRLOIH), and chicagology's witnesses use the second floor throughout — 'a stairway in this hall led to the second floor'.

construction.note: DISPUTED, AND THE DISPUTE HAS A NAME ATTACHED TO IT. Two sources call the Green Tree a two-storey frame building outright. Against that, chicagology's Town of Chicago page reports that W. H. Stow — the man who built the Western Hotel two blocks south — 'did claim that the Green Tree was originally of logs and it was not until years afterward that it was covered with weatherboarding and given the appearance of a frame building.' Frame is adopted because it is the reading of both detailed accounts and because the interior the witnesses describe is a framed interior: board partitions, a stair hall, whitewashed plank walls, chambers laid out on a 12 ft module. The log-core claim is one man's recollection, recorded second-hand, about a rival's house, and it is carried in this record as log_core so it is not lost. Braced versus balloon is separately unattested: balloon framing appeared in Chicago in 1832-33, so an 1833 building could be either, and braced_frame is the conservative reading for the earlier date.

log_core.note: Records the rejected reading so it stays visible. W. H. Stow claimed the Green Tree was originally of logs and weatherboarded only years later. Adopted as false for the reasons in the construction note; if it is true, the 1835 building is a weatherboarded log structure rather than a frame one, which changes the wall section but not the massing, the plan or the placement.

cladding.note: Not directly attested for this building. Clapboard is the standard cladding for a frame building of this type and period, and the competing log-core account calls the covering 'weatherboarding', which is the same thing under another name — so both readings of the construction converge on a lapped horizontal board exterior.

paint.note: A CORRECTION TO A CLAIM IN CIRCULATION. The Green Tree is sometimes described as whitewashed, including in this project's own research summary, but the attested whitewash is INTERIOR: Edwin Gale writes that 'The walls, ceilings, and board partitions had evidently received a coat of whitewash when the house was built'. Nothing describes the exterior finish. Unpainted weathered clapboard is the reading adopted, and it is positively supported by the Sauganash's white paint being remarkable at Wolf Point in 1831 — if the Green Tree had been painted white two years later, the contrast the sources draw would be weaker. Not attested either way; the c. 1859 photograph would settle it.

wall_height_m.note: THE BEST-FOUNDED WALL HEIGHT IN THE DATASET, because a ceiling height is actually attested: 'Seven and one-half feet is rather low for a hotel ceiling.' Two storeys at 7 1/2 ft = 15 ft, plus floor structure between them and a sill course, gives about 16 1/2 ft = 5.0 m to the plate. The 7 1/2 ft is documented; the allowance for joists and sill is the inference.

roof_type.note: John Gray: 'There should also be a small attic window in the gable end, for we used the attic, too.' A gable end with a window in it is a direct attestation of the roof form — one of the few in this dataset that is not typological. With the front on Canal and the long side on Lake, the gable ends face east and west and the ridge runs east-west along Lake Street.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested. 38 degrees is mid-range for period gable framing and leaves an attic tall enough to lodge people in, which the sources say it did.

fenestration.note: The PANE CHARACTER is attested — a guest chamber 'about 12x12, with two windows 6x8', small-paned sash, plus 'a small attic window in the gable end'. Two windows per 12 ft chamber on a 40 x 25 ft two-storey block implies a regularly fenestrated elevation. Since T-0083 the ARRANGEMENT is carried by elevation_scheme, read off plate '11'; this value still states the pane character, which the plate agrees with — 6-over-6 sash in even bays.

elevation_scheme.note: THE BUILDING FRONTS ON A GABLE END, AND ITS EVEN BAYS RUN ALONG THE EAVES ELEVATIONS. Two halves, separately grounded. That the front is a gable end is a join of attested facts already in this record: the front on Canal (F. H. Taylor), the long side on Lake, and the gable ends facing east and west (John Gray's attic window note, and the roof_type note's own reading). The bay ARRANGEMENT — even 6-over-6 sash in regular bays along the long elevation, doors and attic lights on the gable faces — is read off plate '11' of the owner's 2026-08-11 reference set, committed at data/sources/assets/prefire_views_kevin_2026_08/p6_0.png: a tier-5 retrospective view, which may drive fenestration rhythm as inferred and may never drive a coordinate. The plate is not yet held as a source record (T-0075 owns that), so the citation is a committed path. The pictured south eaves elevation's bay count is now stated separately by eaves_bays on T-2376; the opposite elevation keeps the archetype's footprint arithmetic as a reconstruction under docs/LIBERTIES.md L152. No dimension or geographic placement is taken from the plate.

side_entrance.note: PICTURE-LED SOUTH EAVES OPENING PATTERN FOR THE 1835 MODEL, not a finding that this inn never had a side door. The held Andreas/Braunhold reproduction shows seven sash on the south long elevation on each floor, with a sash at the middle ground-floor station. The independently held original Trowbridge plate in Gale 1902, facing p.35 / scan n55, captioned 'The Green Tree Tavern in 1835', shows the same seven-bay window rhythm and no middle ground-floor door; its frontmost lower sash is partly obscured by the hanging board and people, while the middle station is visible. Setting this existing attribute to null selects the archetype's normal sash at all seven existing south-wall stations instead of substituting a door at the fourth station. The earlier John Gray testimony is retained here verbatim: 'on the Lake street front about the middle of the long side', with the hall and stairway behind it (chicagology_prefire127, transcribing the Inter Ocean, 1 July 1883; Gray kept the inn in 1838-41). That later recollection may describe a changed or schematic form, but it does not date the door to 1 July 1835, and the drawings do not prove its historical absence on that date. The choice follows the two pictured opening patterns as inferred form; exact July-1835 appearance remains uncertain. The original undated Andreas plate is not dated by the local reproduction's 1838 caption, and Trowbridge is retrospective, not an independent contemporary 1835 survey. Existing south-wall seven-bay count, even spacing, stock sash dimensions and height bands, north-wall rhythm, primary front entrance, footprint, geographic placement and all other form values stay unchanged. No c.1859 check_required photograph or Gray-derived new geometry supplies this correction; the two public-domain picture records supply the visible sash pattern.

chimney_placement.note: END CHIMNEYS AT BOTH GABLES. Plate '11' of the owner's 2026-08-11 reference set (committed at data/sources/assets/prefire_views_kevin_2026_08/p6_0.png, and its sibling Braunhold view written up as image 6 of data/sources/assets/owner_brief_2026_08_18/README.md) draws one stack at each end of the ridge — a tier-5 retrospective view driving massing as inferred. The plates are not yet held as source records (T-0075), so the citation is a committed path. This replaces the archetype's frontage-fraction arrangement, which on this deeper-than-wide footprint had left both stacks standing OFF the ridge on the roof slopes — the before frame of T-0083 shows it. The COUNT stays the chimneys attribute's own inference; docs/LIBERTIES.md L21 (the town chimney arrangement) and L152 say what is invented here.

rear_ell.note:
T-2376 retires the old rear ell as a July-1835 depiction choice. Its original position was a reconstruction made under the obsolete Canal placement, using the pictured lower wing and Gray's later testimony without a dated rear plan. The governing drawings do not resolve or show that projecting right/rear form. Gray explicitly recalls a right addition 'the same as on the left' during his 1838–41 tenancy, and the historical note promised a second wing if the Lake-and-West-Water placement won; that later bilateral testimony and the promise remain counterevidence, not proof that either addition was absent in 1835 or that both were the same pictured building. The revised model builds the pictured left connector/range, keeps the competing shoulder readings, and leaves an unverified 1835 rear/bilateral stage unmodeled rather than presenting the old placement proxy as another established wing. No historic absence, alteration date, tenant identity or room count is asserted.

HISTORICAL PRE-RETIREMENT NOTE:
THE LOW ADDITION, BUILT AT THE REAR AND DECLARED. John Gray, landlord 1838-41, attests 'a low one-story addition to the right, the same as on the left'; the 1838 Braunhold engraving (owner_brief_2026_08_18 README, image 6) draws 'a lower gabled wing at the left with a wide (carriage) door', and plate '11' (prefire_views_kevin_2026_08/p6_0.png) draws the low gabled wing with the ship masts behind it. WHETHER A WING STOOD ON 1835-07-01 IS NOT ATTESTED — Gray describes the house three to six years after the scene date — so this is a reconstruction under the owner's 2026-08-18 standing ruling, sized by the views and claimed at docs/LIBERTIES.md L152. WHY THE REAR END AND ONLY THE REAR: Gray names additions at BOTH ends, but this record's committed placement puts the west face ON Canal Street's east frontage with zero offset, so the street end has no ground to build on — only the east (rear, yard) end does. That asymmetry is itself evidence worth recording: a west wing fits the ground only under the 'Lake and West Water' placement reading the position note carries as this record's largest residual uncertainty. If that reading ever wins, the second wing goes up with the move. The wing the views draw beside masts is consistent with either.

gallery.note: NO EVIDENCE EITHER WAY, and unlike the Sauganash there is no retrospective depiction in the project's hands to reason from. The witnesses describe two entrances — the front on Canal and one 'about the middle of the long side' on Lake — without mentioning a porch, veranda or gallery, which is weak negative evidence at best, since they were correcting a drawing rather than inventorying the elevation. False is the default, not a finding. The c. 1859 photograph (chm_green_tree_1859) settles this the moment anyone opens it.

side_additions.note: John Gray, landlord 1838-41, correcting a drawing of the house: 'There should also be a low one-story addition to the right, the same as on the left.' So by the end of the 1830s the two-storey core had a low single-storey addition at each end. WHETHER THEY EXISTED ON 1835-07-01 IS NOT ATTESTED — Gray's testimony describes the building three to six years after the scene date — which is why this is inferred and why the additions stay out of the footprint polygon. SINCE T-0083 the rear (east) one is BUILT, at the reconstructed tier, as form.rear_ell — see that attribute for why only the rear end has ground to build on. This value stays the testimony record for BOTH ends; the street-end addition remains unbuilt.

chimneys.note: Not attested in text. A tavern with a bar-room at one end, a parlour, a dining room clearable for dancing and chambers above needed more than one fireplace, and two stacks is the normal disposition for a 40 ft block with a central hall. The number is inference — and since T-0083 it agrees with plate '11', which draws exactly two. WHERE they stand is carried by chimney_placement.

siding_exposure_m.note: INVENTED WITHIN A STOCK SET, NOT DERIVED. No source states the exposed face of any Chicago building's siding. The value is one of four period mill sidings — 4.5, 5, 5.5 or 6 in to the weather; this record wears 5 in — dealt by tools/deal_siding_stock.py: keyed to the phase's construction season, because buildings sided from the same season's shipments of St Joseph sawn lumber tend toward one stock, then advanced so no frame building within 60 m shares this one's. The separation is the surface variety T-0049 reconstructs, not a claim about 1835. docs/LIBERTIES.md L148 owns the invention.

eaves_bays.note: Seven opening stations are drawn on the visible long elevation in the public-domain Andreas/Braunhold plate, held locally as chicago/reference/images/chicago/chicago_green_tree_inn_1838.jpg; the seven upper sash centres are approximately x 822, 928, 1041, 1146, 1243, 1347 and 1443 in its 1600-pixel-wide reproduction. This is tier-5 retrospective form evidence, not a dimension, coordinate or demonstrated 1835 elevation. The existing west-facing gable and Lake Street south-side reading assign that pictured long wall to local x_min; no position or footprint changes. The opposite x_max face is not overridden and retains its six-bay reconstruction. Seven bays fit the existing 12.19 m length at about 1.74 m per bay, keeping the archetype's existing 0.85 m sash and 1.35 m height. Their equal spacing, vertical bands and hidden treatment remain reconstructed. The earlier form replaced the middle lower sash with Gray's textually described south-side entrance. The current T-2376 picture-priority choice uses the existing side_entrance:null option to retain that seventh sash. Gray's later entrance recollection remains explicit counterevidence: no alteration date or absence of that door on 1 July 1835 is established. Other gable, wing and attic-light differences are classified in the individual picture match records.

gable_wall_cladding.note: The pictured main gable continues the framed wall’s horizontal clapboard above the eaves; it is not roof covering. The main-block end triangles now use the existing wall finish and existing reconstructed siding course stock. This switch covers both main gables for a closed model: continuing the pictured finish around the unseen/opposite end is reconstructed, not independently attested. Existing footprint, placement, eave/ridge geometry, roof pitch and covering, course stock and all subsidiary roofs remain unchanged. It does not settle the provisional camera or any remaining opening, roof, wing or grouped-annex differences.

front_ground_layout.note: Two sash left of a rightmost front-gable entrance agree in the actually viewed Andreas 1884 p634/n1301 plate, Trowbridge/Gale 1902 plate facing p35/n55, and Kurz & Allison 1893 panel11. This is retrospective form agreement, not independent contemporaneous proof of 1 July 1835; Kurz may derive from Andreas and Trowbridge may rely on later material. The ascending LOCAL-u fractions are door .20, sash .50, sash .78: exterior +y viewers see higher u toward screen left, so this yields two screen-left sash and a screen-right entrance. Exact centre fractions .20/.50/.78 across the existing 7.62 m wall, equal existing .85x1.35 m sash and 1.20x2.10 m door stock, sill bands, sections and hidden joinery are RECONSTRUCTED, not measured or attested by those pictures. Only the +y front ground floor opts in. The current two upper sash versus Trowbridge's three, attic light, text-attested south-side door, disputed additions, roof, geographic placement and all existing source/camera uncertainties stay unresolved. The held-rights/unverified 1859 source is excluded as a geometry witness. Original T-2376 remains open/differs; this is not a solved camera or picture match. The same pure resolved_front_ground_stations dataclass property (whose actual values are covered by the existing native mesh recipe) is consumed by the mesh and the native entrance/apron/clearance reader after resolving exactly the sidecar-selected source phase; no renderer facade API or bearing is changed.

CURRENT CLOSED-SHOULDER WORKING READING: Andreas's detailed retrospective engraving supplies a closed clapboard shoulder with a lower sash and small front-gable light, followed by a low connector and farther turned gabled range. The existing shoulder_enclosed option is now true. Trowbridge/Gale's captioned1835 drawing instead shows an open post-and-roof wagon bay. That remains explicit counterevidence, not a demonstrated conversion year; the current choice is an evidence-bounded reconstruction of the July1835 scene. The independently drawn open shed/posts and its covered wagon are declined together by the yard source owner while this same canonical attribute is true, rather than drawn inside the closed shoulder.

 Every metric span, hidden depth, height, slope, opening station/section, local placement, plan turn, timber and colour choice remains exactly the existing reconstructed group. No new number, measured plan, surveyed coordinate, historical interior, occupant or extra lodging capacity is inferred. The main footprint and world placement are unchanged. The actual fixed-camera comparison now includes the closed wall, sash and dormer; left-cluster roof silhouette and relative proportions still differ. Original T-2376 remains open/differs. The earlier open-bay model rationale is preserved verbatim in docs/RESEARCH/green-tree-annex-T-2376/previous-open-reading-20261103.md.

 SHOULDER DORMER CAP, 2026-11-04: front_gable_peak_m is raised 4.50 to 4.85 m so the little front-gable light over the closed shoulder reads as the sharply pointed cap Andreas draws, rather than the blunt, nearly flat cap the 4.50 m value produced. Against the builder's existing 4.20 m dormer head and its 0.625 m roof half-span that turns the cap from about 25.6 to about 46.1 degrees. 4.85 m is a RECONSTRUCTED working control chosen for the drawn triangular shape; it is not a measurement off the retrospective plate, which carries no scale, dimension or camera, and it dates nothing. The shoulder roof silhouette and the left group's relative proportions remain OPEN on T-2376.

 SHOULDER ROOF RISE TRIAL, 2026-11-09: the existing roof_high_m working control rises from 4.0 to 4.6 m at the main-block attachment, retaining the outer roof_low_m 3.2 m. Across the unchanged 3.6 m shoulder span this steepens the shed from about 12.5 to 21.3 degrees, following the stronger rise toward the main wall visible behind the little pointed light in Andreas. These are RECONSTRUCTED trial controls for relative form, not dimensions measured from the retrospective drawing, and establish no historical alteration or July-1835 stage. The accepted 4.85 m pointed cap, its light and lower sash, the 2.8 m shoulder wall, all three component spans/depths/occupied polygons and their turn, the main building and its surveyed placement remain unchanged. Existing source disagreement with Trowbridge’s open bay remains explicit. The actual new native mesh, unchanged-camera comparison and published compound review are still required; original T-2376 remains open and the broader left-group proportions are not signed off by this one slope trial.

T-2376 WHOLE LEFT GROUP, 2026-11-10: rereading the actual verified public-domain Andreas and Kurz pictures reveals two distinct far-left gable peaks: the low foreground range and a higher rear gable behind it. The former single constant-height range omitted that visible shape. A bounded rear raised roof section now sits inside the same range envelope, with reconstructed 1.6 m rear depth, 4.5 m wall and 37 degree roof; the front retains its existing 2.6 m wall and 37 degree roof. The existing range depth increases 3.0 to 3.7 m and its front set-out 1.0 to 1.7 m together, retaining the rear corner and 25 degree turn, bringing the low foreground gable forward. The low connector roof now falls away from the main block toward that foreground range, following the pictured link instead of the previous reversed wedge; its working upper edge is 3.0 m and lower edge remains 2.25 m. Existing stock clapboard continues over the shoulder and link upper infill, where the old proxy left a plain patch. Every new metric is RECONSTRUCTED, chosen for bounded relative form rather than measured from a retrospective picture; no historical alteration date, extra room or occupant, site move, new surveyed outline or grade is asserted. Andreas and Kurz may be dependent; Trowbridge’s competing open bay and upper/attic count, Gray’s later side entrance and bilateral additions, and the held c1859 catalogue lead remain explicit counterevidence. Final native/source pictures and actual app review are owed before acceptance; the old partial statements above are historical, not current blockers by themselves. function.note: In operation as a public house throughout the scene window: bar-room serving as office and reception, dining room cleared for dancing, chambers above and lodging in the attic when full. Renamed the Chicago Hotel by 1844, which is after the scene date and is a change of sign, not of trade.

occupants.note: Ingersoll's tenancy is given as 1834-1837, which covers 1835-07-01, with Martin M. Ford associated. DRLOIH's list — 'initially by David Clark and then by Edward Parsons' — carries no dates and is compatible rather than contradictory: Clark (or Clock) is named elsewhere as the landlord who opened the house in 1833, before Ingersoll.

grade.why: Known from maps or written records; no picture of it has been found.

placement.position_note: PLACED 2026-08-11. THE CORNER IS DOCUMENTED AND THE COORDINATE IS DERIVED, so the tag follows the weaker half. Andreas puts the log jail on 'the northwest corner of the court-house square'. The public square is the block bounded by Randolph Street on the north, Washington Street on the south, Clark Street on the east and LaSalle Street on the west - the block this project's own ground control identifies as such in data/traces/gcp/wright_1834_gcps.json, where LaSalle and Randolph is labelled 'NW corner of the Public Square block' and Clark and Washington 'SE corner of the Public Square block'. Its four inside corners were computed for this parcel from modern OpenStreetMap intersection centres fetched 2026-08-11, offset 12.2 m into the block on each axis, half of an 80 ft street per Hathaway 1834: NW 447538.25 / 4637130.78, NE 447639.27 / 4637130.25, SW 447541.20 / 4637018.49, SE 447639.80 / 4637018.05, which makes the block about 101 x 112 m. The jail's own north-west corner is set on the square's north-west corner, so the footprint origin - which is the building's south-west corner - sits its own depth south of it. THIS IS A CORNER OF A BLOCK, NOT A LOT, so it is a weaker statement than the corner-lot placements elsewhere in this dataset: nothing says how far into the block the building stood, whether it was set back from either street line, or which way it faced. WORKING UNCERTAINTY ABOUT 20 M from the georeference (data/datum.json: 17.5 m RMS on Wright 1834, 3.7 per cent paper stretch), plus an unquantified setback into the block. Facade bearing 0, due north onto Randolph, CONVENTION RATHER THAN EVIDENCE - a jail at the north-west corner could as reasonably have faced west onto LaSalle or inward onto the square, and nothing attests it. The square itself in 1835 was otherwise an open, unimproved prairie block, fenced or not; no fence, path or improvement of the block is modelled. RECONCILED WITH THE COMMITTED PLAT 2026-08-28 (T-0246), AND THE CLAIM DID NOT MOVE - ONLY THE LINE IT WAS DERIVED AGAINST. The method above found the square's north-west corner by taking modern OpenStreetMap intersection centres, fetched 2026-08-11, and stepping 12.2 m into the block on each axis. That is not this project's own Randolph Street: the committed centreline in data/streets/1835.json, offset by half the committed 80 ft corridor, is what tools/generate_plat_lots.py builds every platted block edge from, and it is the line every derived layer in this scene reads. Measured against it with tools/measure_corridor_intrusion.py, this footprint's north wall stood 3.48 m OUT PAST blk_randolph_lasalle's Randolph frontage line, in the platted roadway, with its centroid inside the corridor - deeper than any of the four Lake Street records T-0196 looked at - and tools/generate_frontage_works.py refused two steps of Randolph's plank walk, 0.0 to 10.4 m along that face, naming this building in the refusal. THE REPAIR IS THIS RECORD'S OWN METHOD RUN AGAINST THIS PROJECT'S OWN LINE: the footprint is translated 4.981 m along the face's inward normal - dE -0.040 m, dN -4.981 m in local ENU, so UTM E 447538.25 N 4637126.21 becomes E 447538.21 N 4637121.23 - which leaves its north wall 1.50 m back from the committed frontage line. THE SQUARE IS NOT SUBDIVIDED, so there is no lot line to stand off: 1.50 m is plat_occupancy.LOT_MARGIN_M, the plat module's own margin off a boundary, and it is the same figure the reconciled South Water and Lake records took off their lot lines (T-0127, T-0198, T-0199). NOTHING ALONG THE STREET MOVED: the along-face position, the block, the corner and the side are untouched, and so is the confidence grade - re-deriving a coordinate from better geometry is not new evidence, and Andreas's 'northwest corner of the court-house square' is what it always was. WHAT THIS DOES NOT REPAIR: the 20 m working uncertainty stated above is unchanged and dwarfs this 4.98 m, so the move is a reconciliation between two of this project's own lines and not a claim to have located the jail better. The facade bearing stays 0 while this face runs at 0.46 degrees, which leaves the front wall between 1.50 and 1.55 m back across its width; that skew is not corrected here, because rotating a record is a second claim and this one is a repair. V4 ENCLOSURE/ACCESS RECONSTRUCTION 2026-10-30: the earlier exact northing was a chosen setback derived from the public-square street line, not an attested building coordinate. Andreas attests the northwest part of the square, not the exact setback. This finite R placement allows the existing1.80 m native doorway approach plus0.25 m to the continuous palisade axis atN-269.25 (0.16 m beyond a180 mm backing post), rather than preserving an invented centre gap that is absent from the1902 drawing. placement.symbolic_location: North-west corner of the court-house square (the public square bounded by Randolph, Clark, Washington and LaSalle), at the Randolph and LaSalle end; fronting north onto Randolph.

footprint.note: INVENTED. NO SOURCE REACHED GIVES THIS BUILDING A DIMENSION, a plan, or a number of cells. 6.096 x 4.572 m is 20 x 15 ft, recorded converted with the original figures stated per data/datum.json's units rule. The only constraint the evidence offers is relative and it runs in both directions: the jail was built because something more metropolitan was required than the estray pen, so it is a more substantial thing than a stock pound; and it was itself superseded within a few years, so it was small. A 20 x 15 ft log box is a two-cell lock-up and is the smallest thing that answers both. Nothing else about the shape is a finding: the plain rectangle, the proportion and the scale are all this record's.

construction.note: The building is named a LOG jail in the only description this project has of it, which makes the material the single best-attested thing about it. THE PLATE NOW SETTLES THE SECOND HALF OF IT: the engraving of the first Cook County jail in the owner's 2026-08-18 brief (data/sources/assets/owner_brief_2026_08_18/README.md, image 1) draws squared timber laid horizontally — 'a low log jail — squared timber, near-flat roof' — which is hewn log in courses with notched corners, exactly what this archetype builds for this value (generators/common/logwork.py). Until 2026-08-21 this note said hewn-versus-round was unattested and the archetype's hewn wall was a convention standing where evidence should be; the plate is that evidence, at tier 5, for the FABRIC and not for any dimension. Whether the walls were single or doubled, and whether they were lined inside, nothing reached says. The plate is a TIER 5 PICTORIAL held here as the brief's written record rather than a committed binary — the images were supplied in-session and T-0075 owns identifying them against the Andreas plate numbering and creating the source record — so it is cited by path, the way this dataset's other brief-driven attributes are (green_tree_tavern chimneys, image 6). The value's own grade is unchanged: 'log' was attested by Andreas before the plate and still is.

roof_type.note: The detailed public-domain Gale/Trowbridge 1902 plate, captioned 1836, depicts a gabled log core behind the palisade. This replaces the earlier roof choice based on a written near-flat summary. Andreas 1884 depicts a conflicting hip/pyramidal cap; that independent picture is retained as a source disagreement. roof_pitch_deg.note: One bounded 28-degree reconstruction of the visibly pitched gable in the full Gale 1902 plate. On the unchanged reconstructed 4.572 m span it rises 1.216 m, rather than the previous 0.486 m cap. The drawing supplies the taller roof form, not a measured angle, a metric plan or proof of its July 1835 state. The differing Andreas cap does not become a second building.

wall_height_m.note: A finite 3.35 m eave choice exposes 0.91 m of core above the existing reconstructed 2.44 m palisade, as both retrospective pictures show a substantial log block above the enclosure. This replaces the previous archetype-default 2.66 m choice, which hid almost all wall fabric. Neither plate measures metres; exact height and July continuity are reconstruction. No footprint, site coordinate, street control, storey count or separate later cell is added.

door.note: Not attested. `door` in this archetype names what has to get through the opening rather than whether there was one. A jail takes a person through in hand and nothing else - no horse, no wagon - so the man-door class is the reading, and it is the only one whose 1.88 m clear height fits under this wall. Where the door stood, what it was made of, and whether it was barred or grated is not attested and is the archetype's default.

picture_layout.note: The detailed public-domain 1902 plate shows one upright barred-looking light in the log gable beside the keeper house. The light sits on the east end facing the keeper-house side: 0.48 x 0.85 m dark recess, three uprights, one horizontal crossbar, 55 mm frame, head 0.73 m above eave. These metric choices, count of uprights, material, compass and July continuity are not measured or attested. The opening does not assert a second storey or hay loft. Other outbuildings retain their default layout.

function.note: Purpose-built for confinement, and it is the building that ended the practice recorded on the estray_pen record - prisoners held in the stock pound for want of anywhere else. Cook County was organised in 1831 and the county's business was conducted in rented rooms; this is the first purpose-built county structure of any kind and it precedes the court-house on the same block by about two years.

footprint.note: THE TWO-MASS PLAN, AND THE 12 x 8 m PLACEHOLDER IS RETIRED (T-0626, spending T-0617's reading). THE FRONTAGE IS DERIVED AND THE DEPTH IS NOT, and the block is graded at the weaker of the two. FRONTAGE 9.92 m: Braunhold's engraving draws five bays on the street face and rectified against that face's own vanishing point the five are EQUAL to 2.4 % (tools/measure_sauganash_plate.py, bay_rhythm.rectified_gaps 0.997 / 1.011 / 1.020 / 0.972). The bay measures 1.984 m at the plate's stated scale datum — a standing adult at 1.70 m, hat included, the two men on the walk reading 147 and 143 px — so five bays are 9.92 m. THE DATUM'S BIAS IS SMALL AND BOUNDED, which is what makes this a measurement rather than a floor: the men stand a pace forward of the wall, and the plate's own focal length puts them 43.0 m from the station (f 3664.7 px on a 145 px figure of 1.70 m), so a pace is 2.7 %. The frontage is therefore 9.9-10.2 m and 12 m IS REFUTED rather than merely unsupported. The value taken is the measured 9.92 and is not fudged up into the correction. What does still move it is the 1.70 m datum itself: at 1.60 m the frontage reads 9.3 m and at 1.80 m 10.5 m. DEPTH 8.0 m IS UNCHANGED AND IS STILL A RECONSTRUCTION. One plate gives no depth (docs/RESEARCH/sauganash_image_accuracy.md row 11), so nothing has measured it; it is held at the placeholder's own figure deliberately, because the placement above offsets this origin by the footprint's own 8 m depth to stand the north face on the Lake Street frontage, and moving a number with no evidence behind it would move the building. That the building was a two-storey white frame block is documented (Wau-Bun); how big it was is measured off one retrospective sheet and no better. The renderer therefore does NOT dither the massing on account of this tag — see generators/archetypes/frame_tavern.py — and the dimensional uncertainty is carried in the sidecar instead.

construction.note: Balloon framing was developed in Chicago in 1832-33 and became the dominant local method. This building predates that by a year, so balloon framing is the LESS likely reading: a braced frame built onto a log core is more probable for 1831. Flagged for correction — the value is retained only until the framing question is researched, and it should probably become braced_frame. Do not treat this as settled.

cladding.note: Implied by 'white' painted finish on a frame building; clapboard is the standard cladding for the type and period. Not directly attested.

The DIMENSION remains uncertain; what is inferred is that it falls in this range, not that it is exactly 5.5 m.

fenestration.note: No period source describes the window arrangement. A regular five-bay elevation with a centred entrance is the standard disposition for a building of this size and type, and both retrospective depictions show regular bays. Braunhold's street face detects five openings in the upper storey and five in the ground storey, with the door the MIDDLE of the five — the darkest opening on the ground storey at ink 0.494, and nothing else on the sheet is inked like an open door onto an unlit room. The five are EQUAL: drawn gaps of 169.2, 161.1, 153.0 and 137.5 px are a 20.4 % spread that reads as an irregular rhythm and is not one, rectifying to 0.997, 1.011, 1.020 and 0.972 against the face's own vanishing point. Brick is also the plausible reading on its own terms: a hotel raised in 1831 at the settlement's centre, when brick was reaching Chicago in trade, and no period text describes the stacks either way. A single tier-5 view may drive a material as inferred; the brief's binaries are not yet committed, so the citation is the README until T-0075 lands identifications.

cross_wing.note: THE SECOND TWO-STOREY MASS, AND THE PLATE PROVES IT BY ARITHMETIC. The owner reported it missing on 2026-09-03 from the dev preview: 'i think there is a structure missing but you have it on the front and they have it on the rear in pictures, and it looks like the full height of the main building and similar design as the main building appears to be almost the same size, it connects from the back and side in the images.' T-0617 measured the near apex at (648, 350) with one line running out of it at image slope -0.318 and one at +0.095, and called the right-hand one a ridge on the strength of the asymmetry alone. T-0626 finished the sum. Project each line onto the vertical through the vanishing point of the plane it lies in — the plate gives both horizontal vanishing points and its own focal length, recovered from their orthogonality — and BOTH come out horizontal in the world: 1.35 deg and 0.11 deg, where a 38 deg rake in the same plane would have been DRAWN at image slope -1.99 against the -0.318 measured. So they are two RIDGES meeting at one apex, not a ridge and a rake, and the mass the owner reported is on the sheet as a measurement rather than as an impression. tools/sauganash_apex_lines.py is that arithmetic and tools/check.sh gates on it. THE SHARED APEX IS ALSO WHAT SIZES THE WING: two gable ridges of one wall height and one pitch meet at a point only when they span the same width, so the wing's span is this block's own depth and the archetype refuses to build it at any other. GRADE. One sheet — Braunhold's. The Petford watercolour and the Trowbridge drawing are the same composition from the same station, so they copy it rather than corroborate it (docs/RESEARCH/sauganash_image_accuracy.md section 1), and a tier-5 retrospective that passes its own perspective test may be read for PROPORTION and never for a coordinate. CITED ON BRAUNHOLD ALONE. The Petford and Trowbridge views were dropped from this row on 2026-09-04 for the reason the reading itself gives: they are the same composition from the same station, so listing them would dress a copy as a corroboration. The earlier separate rights concern is now superseded by verified 1902 publication, but the dependence argument still applies: a later copy is not independent corroboration.

cross_wing_end.note: WHICH END IS DECIDED BY THE PLAT, NOT BY THE PLATE. All three views put the tall wing and the log annex at the LEFT of the composition, at the same end of the building; nothing in any of them says which real end of it that is, and a retrospective view may not drive a coordinate in any case. The lot decides. This phase's placement stands the block's WEST face on Market Street's east kerb line at a 0 m setback, so a wing at the west end would stand in Market Street. It goes at the EAST end — x_max in the archetype's local frame — which is also the end the log annex already stands against: data/structures/philo_carpenter_log_shop.json is set hard on this block's east face, by the same elimination and stated there since 2026-08-11. Graded inferred, because the premise the elimination runs on — a 0 m setback from an 80 ft platted street — is itself the placement's own inference. NO SOURCES ON THIS ROW, DELIBERATELY: it cites nothing because it rests on nothing new. The plat equivalence, the kerb line and the 0 m setback are all this phase's own position block, which carries its sources; repeating them here would claim a second, independent standing this row does not have.

cross_wing_depth_m.note: INVENTED WITHIN A BOUND, AND IT IS THE ONLY NUMBER ON THIS MASS THAT IS. How far the wing runs BACK is what one sheet cannot give (docs/RESEARCH/sauganash_image_accuracy.md row 11): from the plate's station the wing stands behind the main block with only its ridge showing, so the drawing carries its height and its direction and not its length. 8.0 m is the owner's own reading of the views — 'almost the same size' as the main block — taken as equal to the block's 8 m depth, which is also the span the shared apex forces on the wing, so the wing comes out square in plan. docs/LIBERTIES.md L217 owns the invention. The number was also chosen to leave the fenced rear yard, its Market Street gateway and its three kept trees their room: nothing about that yard is attested either, and a wing sized to fill it would be one guess crowding another.

function.note:
A tavern from 1829 and a hotel from 1831; the social centre of the settlement in the target window. Chicago's first billiard table in a public house stood here.

THE HOUSE IS OPEN, AND FRESHLY DONE UP, THREE WEEKS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE. Reviewing the town's public houses against Detroit's new American Hotel, the Chicago Democrat of 10 June 1835, page 2 column 5, claim chicago_democrat_1835_06_10#c001, reports that 'The Sauganash has been re[paired,] fitted up and furnished with neatness and [taste,] and so far as it goes, will[, we have no doubt,] be found just the thing'. That is the only dated statement of this building's CONDITION the corpus holds, and it bears on how the scene should read it: on 1835-07-01 the Sauganash is a working, recently refitted public house and not the shabby survivor its 1829 log origins invite. 'so far as it goes' is the editor's qualification and it means small — his complaint in the same paragraph is that no establishment in Chicago is 'sufficiently extensive'. The refit is recorded here rather than in the form block below because nothing in it names a fabric, a storey or a colour, and inventing one from 'fitted up' is exactly the supply this project refuses.

occupants.note: The Beaubiens owned it until 1834; the hotel chronology gives 'Davis (1835)' as operator, possibly the John Davis running the Steamboat Hotel on North Water Street. Mark Beaubien himself had moved on by the scene date — he built the Exchange Coffee House at Lake and Wells in 1834. The 1835 proprietor is a lead, not a settled fact.

built.note: Wau-Bun, describing 1831: 'a house just completed by Mark Beaubien.'

placement.position_note: PLACED 2026-08-11, AND UNIQUELY IN THIS PARCEL IT IS PLACED AGAINST ANOTHER BUILDING RATHER THAN AGAINST A STREET. The sources give a relation, not an address: a log building on Lake Street near the river, 'immediately adjacent to the Sauganash's public bar' (docs/research/03-structures-north.md section 1), and since 2026-09-04 also drloih_beaubien's 'his original log cabin, adjacent to his Sauganash Tavern'. So this position is derived from data/structures/sauganash_hotel.json's own placement and inherits every uncertainty in it. MOVED 2.08 M WEST ON 2026-09-04 (T-0626), and only because the wall it is set against moved: the Sauganash's frame_1831 footprint stopped being a 12 x 8 m placeholder and became a measured 9.92 x 8 m block, so its east face came in from E 447186.1 to E 447184.02 and this shop came with it. Nothing here is a new claim about where the shop stood; it is the same claim re-derived from a corrected wall. THE SAUGANASH'S PLACEMENT, RESTATED SO THIS RECORD CAN BE RE-DERIVED: the Sauganash stands at the south-east corner of Lake and Market, its frame_1831 footprint origin at EPSG:26916 E 447174.1, N 4637265.2, 9.92 m wide and 8 m deep with a facade bearing of 0, so its north face is on the Lake Street frontage at N 4637273.2 and its east face at E 447184.02. THIS SHOP IS SET HARD AGAINST THAT EAST FACE, its own west wall on E 447184.02 and its north face on the same Lake Street frontage, which is what 'immediately adjacent' means and is why the two footprints touch. WHICH SIDE THE BAR WAS ON IS NOT ATTESTED and the east side is chosen by elimination: the Sauganash's west face stands on the Market Street frontage, so there is no room for a building there at all. THAT ELIMINATION NOW CARRIES A SECOND BUILDING TOO. Until 2026-09-04 this note read that the retrospective depictions put the surviving 1829 log wing on the hotel's LEFT FRONT, 'which is the Market side', and the hotel's own record drew a log wing there. Both were wrong in the same way: the views are drawn from a station, not from a compass, and a log annex on the Market side would stand in Market Street exactly as a shop would. The annex at the left of every view IS THIS BUILDING — drloih_beaubien captions the engraving 'The log cabin on the left was Chicago's first drugstore' — so the hotel's log_wing attribute is retired and the hotel's second, TALL wing takes the same east end, standing back off the rear beside this cabin. WORKING UNCERTAINTY ABOUT 20 M, the georeference's residual (data/datum.json, 17.5 m RMS), carried in from the Sauganash rather than added to; the 2.08 m correction above is inside it many times over and changes nothing about what this record knows. Facade bearing 0, north onto Lake Street, and the 20 ft dimension is set along the street with the 16 ft as the depth — the same convention hogan_store's record argues for and, like it, an inference rather than evidence. Turning the shop through 90 degrees would make it a 16 ft frontage 20 ft deep, and nothing decides.
placement.symbolic_location: Lake Street near the river, on the south side, immediately east of and against the Sauganash Hotel — the source says immediately adjacent to the Sauganash's public bar.

footprint.note: THE SECOND BUILDING FOOTPRINT IN THIS DATASET THAT IS EVIDENCE RATHER THAN A PLACEHOLDER, after Hogan's store. Andreas gives the size: a 16 x 20 ft log building. 16 x 20 ft is 4.877 x 6.096 m, recorded converted with the original figures stated, per data/datum.json's units rule. WHAT IS DOCUMENTED IS THE SIZE AND NOT THE PLAN: '16 x 20' is a rectangle in any reading and this polygon is that rectangle, but nothing attests a door, a counter, or that the building was exactly rectangular rather than a rectangle with a shed on the back. WHICH AXIS RUNS ALONG THE STREET IS NOT IN THE SOURCE either; it is decided by the facade bearing and argued in the position note, where it belongs. This is the smallest building in the dataset — 30 square metres, a single pen — and that is worth reading twice: Chicago's first drug store was a room.

construction.note: Andreas: a log building. No source describes the corner treatment, the chinking or whether any of it was sided; the archetype builds hewn log, which is the commonest construction at the forks in 1832 and what the source names.

stories.note: Not stated. A 16 x 20 ft single-pen log building is single-storey by type, and a two-storey building on that plan would be a tower. Inference from the documented dimensions, which is as close to derivation from evidence as this dataset's storey counts get.

wall_height_m.note: No figure is attested. 2.5 m is about 8 ft: one storey of hewn log wall at typical period course counts, plus a sill. The same reading and the same number this project gives Hogan's store and the Walker meeting house.

roof_type.note: Not attested. Gable is the near-universal roof form for log construction of this type, period and region. A shed roof leaning on the Sauganash's east wall is the one plausible alternative — 'immediately adjacent' could describe a lean-to — and it is recorded here rather than built, because nothing in the sources describes the junction between the two buildings.
